IND.name: India
IND.summary:
India is elevated-risk for trans visitors, with a complex mix of constitutional protection and real practical gaps. The Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA judgment affirmed a constitutional right to self-determined gender identity, and the 2019 Act provides third-gender recognition. But a 2026 amendment bill — passed by parliament — has been called a "huge setback" by Human Rights Watch: it removes the self-identification right and narrows the legal definition.

Police abuse is documented (a trans woman was groped by a railway-protection constable to "check gender"; TheProbe documents police atrocities), airport security discriminated against a trans student at Chennai (CISF), passport authorities have demanded unwarranted medical exams, and a new penal code removed safeguards protecting trans people from sexual violence. Enforcement is uneven — only 11 of 36 states and territories have transgender protection cells.

India has no trans-murder toll comparable to Brazil and courts are protective, but the police abuse + amendment setback + safeguard removal + enforcement gaps + airport and passport friction place it in the Elevated-Risk band. Huge subnational variation is expected: liberal metros like Bangalore and Kerala are materially safer than conservative rural north and central states.
IND.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (theft, scams, sexual harassment of women tourists) is a documented concern in India affecting all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

CHN.name: China
CHN.summary:
China is elevated-risk — authoritarian but not criminalising. The most directly visitor-specific finding is airport discrimination: a Thai trans YouTuber was singled out and subjected to discriminatory treatment at a Chinese airport. The most severe documented case is forced psychiatric commitment: a trans woman was held for 97 days and subjected to electroshock "conversion" therapy under family pressure (she won unprecedented compensation), showing the medical/psychiatric system can be weaponized — though this targeted a resident, not a tourist.

Under Xi Jinping, the space for LGBTQ+ organising and expression is shrinking: Pride-month social-media and film censorship, a government crackdown on LGBT NGOs (2023), a performance ban on transgender TV icon Jin Xing, and cancellation of a foreign drag queen's tour. There is no criminalisation of trans identity, no bathroom restriction law, and courts can provide some protection, but there are no anti-discrimination protections.

China is a regional gender-affirming-care hub, but the parental-consent barrier applies even to adults.
CHN.outOfScopeNotes: General state surveillance, internet censorship, and arbitrary-detention risks affect all travellers to China; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.summary:
Malaysia is high-risk — one of the few countries that criminalises gender expression per se. All 13 states and the Federal Territory prohibit "a man posing as a woman" under Sharia law (up to 3 years in jail, a fine, and caning). While these laws technically apply to Muslims, the enforcement climate affects all trans people: religious police conduct systematic raids on trans events — tipping off media in advance and sharing detainees' faces with tabloids (public outing and humiliation). Three trans women were killed in fewer than two months in 2019.

The political climate is shifting toward Islamist parties (a deputy minister urged the "deviant culture" label for LGBTQ; state-backed "rehabilitation" programs; dating-site blocking). For a non-Muslim foreign trans visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing law doesn't directly apply, but being caught in a raided venue, facing the enforcement climate, or being subject to Section 377A (same-sex conduct, 20 years + whipping, applies to all including tourists) are real risks. There is no legal gender recognition.
MYS.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and Islamic-law compliance (alcohol, dress codes for religious sites) affect Muslim and non-Muslim travellers in different ways; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

SGP.name: Singapore
SGP.summary:
Singapore is reduced-risk — far safer than its neighbour Malaysia, with no criminalisation of trans identity, no religious police, and one of the world's lowest crime rates. Section 377A (which criminalised sex between men) was repealed in 2022, and the prison service reports no assaults against its 10 transgender inmates — unusually positive for axis-H. Singapore is also a regional medical hub with gender-affirming care available.

The main gaps: legal gender recognition requires genital surgery (expensive and restrictive), there is no anti-discrimination law (the 2025 Workplace Fairness Act explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity), and over 65% of trans Singaporeans report negative workplace experiences. A radio code still groups homosexuality with "paedophilia and incest" as lifestyles barred from the airwaves. Progress has "stalled" since the 377A repeal, with discrimination "quietly tolerated."

For a visitor: efficient border processing, very low street crime, unrestricted bathrooms, and no trans-specific police friction. The atmosphere is conservative but quietly accommodating in practice.
SGP.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is extremely low; no trans-specific travel advisory.

IRN.name: Iran
IRN.summary:
Iran is one of the world's most severe environments for trans people — but with a unique bifurcation. Same-sex conduct carries the death penalty, and a trans woman was raped in Ministry of Intelligence custody (the documented case of Ghazal Marzban in Evin Prison, 2023). The Tehran City Council ordered trans people to avoid "busy" areas of the capital. Trans people who have not had surgery face immorality and indecency provisions (imprisonment, fines, lashes) and documented forced-transition pressure — 6Rang describes "40 years of forcing gay people to choose between transitioning and death."

However, transsexuality IS legally recognised in Iran (under a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini), and gender-affirming surgery is state-funded — making Iran one of the few countries in the region with any legal recognition of trans identity, and a trans medical-tourism hub. A post-operative trans visitor with matching documents is in a structurally different and better position than a pre-operative or non-binary visitor, or anyone perceived as same-sex-active — who face the death penalty, state-custody sexual violence, and forced-transition coercion.
IRN.outOfScopeNotes: General state-surveillance risks, compulsory hijab for all women, and the risk of arbitrary detention for foreign nationals affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: RFE/RL (March 2024): Tehran's city council spokesman said transgender people should congregate only in certain parts of the capital and avoid 'busy' areas - official guidance highlighting how the LGBT community is shunned; most LGBT Iranians hide their orientation and lead double lives for fear of persecution.

HRANA (Aug 2026): trans woman Ghazal Marzban, incarcerated in Evin Prison, recounts in a letter that after her May 2023 arrest she was taken blindfolded to a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility, searched, and raped by a masked man; officials promised release in exchange for silence and threatened her against speaking out.

6Rang submission (Feb 2025) to the UN Independent Expert on SOGI, 'They See Us as Criminals: The Forces Driving LGBTIQ+ Displacement from Iran': survey of 25 LGBTIQ+ people who fled Iran (96% from ethnic minorities) documenting systematic persecution driving displacement.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations criminalised with a maximum penalty of death; trans people who have undergone surgery may change legal gender markers but face violence, discrimination and harassment; strict censorship bans LGBTIQ media; the UN Fact-Finding Mission (March 2025) found discriminatory public statements by officials at the highest levels and that LGBTQ+ people arrested in the 2022 protests suffered 'dehumanising insults, threats and treatment amounting to torture'.

UK Home Office CPIN Iran: Sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v5.0, Dec 2025): the Islamic Penal Code criminalises all same-sex activity (flogging to death penalty); no discrimination protections; convictions on pretext of more severe charges; gender reassignment surgery is permitted and may be subsidised after a 'gender identity disorder' diagnosis, but is invasive and often sub-standard; recognition only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution.

LGBTQ Nation (Oct 2025): trans medical tourism is booming in Iran - the government promotes discounted gender-affirming surgery packages to foreigners for currency, while the industry's expertise stems from decades of forcing gay people to choose between transitioning and death; also reports 100 trans inmates presumed dead after an Israeli attack on an Iranian prison.

Business Insider (July 2024): Iran's transgender policy might seem surprisingly liberal - the state pays for gender-transition surgery - but 'it comes at a cost: your dignity'; profiles Shayan Varamini and examines the paradox of state-funded transition alongside criminalisation of homosexuality.

6Rang submission to Iran's UPR (48th session, Jan-Feb 2025): human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people in Iran - documentation of persecution, violence and legal discrimination.

HRW (Nov 2005): 'Iran: Two More Executions for Homosexual Conduct' - documents executions for consensual same-sex conduct under Iran's penal code, part of the pattern of death-penalty application to LGBT people.

IRN.localsOnly: The 1987 fatwa's legal recognition of transsexuality and state-funded gender-affirming surgery are resident-facing; the forced-transition pressure on gay people is a resident phenomenon, though it signals the state's posture.

ISR.name: Israel
ISR.summary:
Israel is the Middle East's most progressive destination for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and Tel Aviv as a regional queer hub.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, Ben-Gurion Airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition ("If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male"). Every foreign visitor transits Ben-Gurion, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Trump's anti-trans rhetoric is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing Netanyahu coalition and the Israel-Hamas war aftermath have weakened protections, though the National Security Committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.
ISR.outOfScopeNotes: Security risks from the Israel-Hamas conflict (rockets, terrorism, border areas) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Directly documents airport-screening problems for trans travellers in Israel.

Jerusalem Post (May 2026): the Aguda's Nir Katz Center 2025 report found 432 homophobic or transphobic physical incidents in Israel in 2025 - a sharp rise, including 'carefully planned lynch ambushes carried out through dating apps', stabbings and extortion.

Ynet (May 2026): Israel's 2025 LGBTQ-phobia report finds record-high anti-LGBTQ violence - at least one physical assault per week; physical attacks rose to half of public-space incidents (from 32%); extortion/threats rose from 3% to 13.5%; 91% of survey respondents experienced LGBTQ-phobia in the past year but only 7% reported it; trans people bear the brunt despite being a minority within the community.

Haaretz (Feb 2025): Trump's anti-trans rhetoric and executive orders are impacting Israel's transgender community - activists report increasing violent rhetoric locally, including transphobia from within the LGBTQ community.

Haaretz (May 2023): Israel Police issued a new regulation for body searches of trans people who have not fully transitioned - male officers will search male genitalia and female officers female genitalia; LGBTQ groups decry the regulation as harmful, humiliating and traumatic (previously officers had to ask the person's preference).

Jerusalem Post (June 2024): the Interior Ministry amended ID regulations so trans people no longer need to register their 'dead name' on their teudat zehut - following a High Court petition by trans woman Nofar Ashbel, who argued that displaying the previous name outed her gender change.

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.summary:
Argentina has one of the world's most progressive legal frameworks — the 2012 Gender Identity Law allows administrative self-identification (no medical requirements), offers an X marker for non-binary people, and funds transition healthcare. Buenos Aires is "one of the safest major cities in Latin America for LGBTQ+ visitors."

But the situation is deteriorating sharply under the Milei government: the president has called "gender ideology" "child abuse," issued decrees modifying the Gender Identity Law, and hate crimes hit a record 227 in 2025 (up 62%, one every 38 hours — trans women bearing the brunt). Police institutional violence against trans and travesti women is documented (arbitrary raids, drug-law criminalisation, searches only on travestis). The violence targets local vulnerable communities rather than tourists, but the trajectory is concerning.

The 2012 self-ID law remains in force for adults and courts are pushing back on the Milei decrees.
ARG.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (robbery, scams) in Buenos Aires affects all tourists; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

ARG.blindLocalsOnly: The decrees banning minors' hormone therapy and surgery, and the prison-housing decree, affect residents; the self-ID law, X marker and state-funded transition healthcare are domestic administrative processes a visitor does not use.
ARG.blindTangential: Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010 (a regional first) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with a same-sex partner.

ARE.name: United Arab Emirates
ARE.summary:
The UAE is one of the most thoroughly documented trans-traveler-hostile countries in the world. At the border, trans visitors have been X-rayed to check their genitals (Israeli trans women, detained and denied entry at Dubai airport), deported for having a male passport (Thai model Rachaya Noppakaroon at Expo 2020; Gigi Gorgeous), denied entry despite valid UAE visas (Indian trans person), and sentenced to prison for "dressing in a feminine way" (Singaporean trans woman, 1 year in Abu Dhabi). A Brazilian trans woman was arrested in her Dubai apartment by plainclothes police accusing her of drug trafficking.

The state "employs various legal mechanisms to explicitly acknowledge and penalize nonconformity with traditional gender roles" and actively targets "non-Emirati tourists." There is no legal gender recognition.

However, the UAE does not have the death penalty for same-sex conduct (unlike Saudi Arabia or Iran), no documented custodial death of a trans person (unlike Saudi), and some trans visitors do enter successfully if their passport gender matches their presentation. The targeting is triggered by passport/presentation mismatch, not blanket.
ARE.outOfScopeNotes: Strict rules on social behaviour, drug possession, and financial crimes (exit bans) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Ynetnews report on two Israeli trans women denied entry to Dubai (2025): detained for hours at the airport, subjected to repeated physical examinations including X-ray checks 'to see whether we had male or female genitals' despite passports listing them as female, mocked by staff, and deported. Illustrates anatomy-based screening of trans travellers at UAE borders.

Vice report (March 2022): Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, travelling with a team of 14 to perform at Expo 2020 Dubai, was stopped at immigration, interrogated for nine hours, and deported despite valid documents - reportedly because her passport still showed her male gender marker.
NOTE: Page content did not load at fetch time (only AP site navigation was retrieved); the specific article content was not retrievable.

Brazilian outlet Metropoles (April 2023, in Portuguese): a Brazilian trans woman was arrested in Dubai in September 2022 after police (investigating her acquaintance for drug trafficking) accused her of drug offences when she failed a toxicological exam; she accuses the Brazilian embassy of negligence. Shows trans visitors can be swept into the UAE criminal system with thin consular support.

Cairo 52 legal review of the UAE: multiple legal mechanisms explicitly penalise non-conformity with traditional gender roles; trans expression (appearance or accessories) frequently leads to arrest, detention or deportation of non-Emirati tourists and residents. Legal gender recognition is severely constrained; a recent medical liability law explicitly prohibits gender-affirming healthcare for non-intersex people. Article 359 and related provisions criminalise cross-dressing and 'imitation of women'.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); Human Dignity Trust country profiles document the criminalisation status and penalties in the jurisdiction.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): the 2022 federal criminal code criminalises consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment (complaint-based enforcement). Article 412 penalises 'any man who disguises himself as a woman to enter a woman-only space' - a provision used to prosecute trans women and gender-nonconforming people. No legal gender recognition; no LGBTI organisations able to register.

TMZ report (Aug 2016): Canadian trans model Gigi Gorgeous was detained at Dubai airport and denied entry; she says the immigration officer told her 'I was told you are transgender. You cannot come into the country.' Dubai authorities cited the passport; 'imitation of women by men' is illegal in Dubai.

Brian Whitaker's overview essay (2016), part 1 of a four-part series on transgender issues in the Middle East: gender segregation and legally enforced dress codes make trans people especially vulnerable; anything blurring the male/female distinction is treated as a threat to social order. Notes 'The Danish Girl' was banned by censors in the UAE, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait, and discusses cross-dressing as a crime across the region.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for the UAE: significant human-rights issues include torture in detention, arbitrary and incommunicado detention, political prisoners, privacy interference, censorship, criminal libel, internet restrictions - the report's sections cover treatment of LGBT persons (criminalisation, morality-based arrests, and enforcement against gender expression).

ARE.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors travelling with a partner, or perceived as same-sex-active.

ZAF.name: South Africa
ZAF.summary:
South Africa has one of the world's most progressive constitutional frameworks for trans rights — it was the first country to ban discrimination on sexual orientation (1996), has a legal gender recognition procedure (the Alteration of Sex Description Act, 2003), marriage equality (2006), and an Equality Act prohibiting unfair discrimination on gender. The Equality Court recently ruled in favour of a trans inmate who was denied gender expression and healthcare in prison (the Mokoena case, November 2025), affirming the constitutional right to gender-affirming healthcare for inmates, and Correctional Services has developed a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners.

But there is a wide gap between law and lived reality. LGR is administratively difficult, expensive, and inconsistently implemented ("the Mariana Trench of transphobia"). A trans woman was brutally attacked in a Tshwane tavern (January 2025); a Grindr-hostage ordeal was reported (December 2024); and anti-transgender violence has been documented within the public health system. There is a legal debate about whether businesses can refuse trans people facility access under the Consumer Protection Act.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, private healthcare available, and Cape Town and Johannesburg have established queer scenes. The violence targets local trans communities, not tourists.
ZAF.outOfScopeNotes: South Africa's high general crime rate (violent crime, carjackings, muggings) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Full judgment: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Equality Court, 10 November 2025): inmates' constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming healthcare for trans inmates for whom it is prescribed; failure to provide it constitutes unfair discrimination and harassment under PEPUDA; refusal to allow feminising clothing, accessories, cosmetics and chosen pronouns also constitutes unfair discrimination and harassment.

Lawyers for Human Rights case summary (Nov 2025): the High Court sitting as an Equality Court ruled for trans inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services - unfair discrimination and harassment for refusing gender expression (feminising attire, 'she/her' pronouns); an inmate's right to 'adequate medical treatment' includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense; DCS ordered to implement accommodations and its own transgender-inmate SOPs.

South African Human Rights Commission media statement (Nov 2025): the National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the Mokoena ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities, in the context of its OPCAT mandate to monitor places of deprivation of liberty.

GroundUp (Aug 2025): transgender prisoners challenge prison authorities - NM, a trans woman in Johannesburg Correctional Centre, has sought gender-affirming healthcare for over five years despite DCS psychiatrist recommendations; her case parallels Jade September's 2019 Equality Court win at Pollsmoor; Correctional Services has a standard operating procedure for trans prisoners but rights organisations are concerned about implementation.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): first country to ban sexual-orientation discrimination in its constitution (1996); adoption 2002, marriage equality 2005/2006; since 2003 trans and intersex people can amend sex markers under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act - but it requires medical evidence, pathologising trans identities; reform toward self-determination not yet adopted as of 2026; the 2024 Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act explicitly recognises SOGISC.

GroundUp opinion (June 2025) by Mikhail Petersen: 'We need to change the law on gender recognition' - ordinary administrative tasks (bank accounts, grants, affidavits, boarding planes) are fraught with risk for trans South Africans without matching ID; documented cases of denied services, detention, fraud accusations; a Gender Dynamix 2024 report case of a trans woman denied the right to open a domestic-violence case and told to 'go home and fight back like a man'.

MambaOnline (Jan 2025): a 23-year-old trans woman, Aobakwe Mahlobo, survived a violent, unprovoked hate-crime attack at a Tshwane tavern (26 December 2024) that left her with severe facial injuries; a man nearby began making hateful comments before assaulting her.

OUT LGBT Well-being / MambaOnline monthly rights watch (December 2024): overview of reported LGBTIQ+ rights violations - including a gay couple in Muldersdrift enduring a three-day hostage ordeal after a Grindr meeting, with alleged police neglect and bias; Pride event highlighting health-access gaps in Buffalo City.

Academic article (PER/PELJ, 2024): 'Did the CPA Shut the Bathroom Doors for Transgender and Non-Binary People?' - critical legal reflection of section 9(2) of the Consumer Protection Act, which permits separate-but-equal facilities for each gender, questioning its impact on trans and non-binary access.

Daily Maverick opinion (Jan 2026) by Mikhail Petersen (Gender Dynamix): 'The dauntingly high cost of affirming your gender in South Africa' - argues for legal gender recognition grounded in human rights and dignity, without requiring expensive, hard-to-access healthcare; opens with the scenario of being stopped at a routine roadblock with mismatched documents.

IOL/SAPA: Justice Minister Jeff Radebe launched a programme against gender-based violence including violence against the LGBTI community - the constitution's equality clause is 'one of the most progressive constitutional provisions in the world', but discrimination and violent attacks persist; a national task team and rapid response team were created to address hate crimes, with a hate-crimes policy framework finalised.

ZAF.tangentialFactors: The Grindr-hostage ordeal (December 2024) is a caution for trans visitors using apps; the facility-access legal debate affects visitors' everyday exposure.
ZAF.localsOnly: The Alteration of Sex Description Act LGR procedure (difficult, expensive, inconsistently implemented) is resident-facing; the Mokoena prison case and the public-health-system violence concern residents.

IDN.name: Indonesia
IDN.summary:
Indonesia is high-risk for trans visitors — with a directly documented trans-traveler death in custody and a presidential decree classifying LGBTQ+ as a national security threat. Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard trans activist from Peru, died in Bali police custody in 2022 after arrest at Bali airport on his honeymoon (family alleges police beating; police deny violence).

In Aceh province, Sharia law criminalises same-sex relations with public caning (applies to all persons in Aceh, including tourists). A new penal code effective January 2026 effectively criminalises all same-sex conduct nationally. President Prabowo in October 2025 classified "promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" as a national security threat alongside terrorism — and vigilante mob attacks on trans women escalated after this decree (10 attacks documented in Bogor between March and July 2026). Police conduct discriminatory raids on gay gatherings (75 arrested in Bogor in June 2025).

BUT: Bali is a major tourist hub where many trans visitors enter discreetly without incident; Indonesia has no death penalty; and Rodrigo's death is disputed (police deny violence) rather than clearly documented state torture.
IDN.outOfScopeNotes: Drug laws are severe (Rodrigo was arrested on drug charges); general terrorism/crime risks in certain regions affect all travellers.

Harvard Crimson (Sept 2022): the mother of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla - a 32-year-old Peruvian trans man and Harvard student - alleges he was arrested at Bali airport on drug charges, subjected to extortion (demands rising from $100,000 to $200,000), and died three days later in hospital while in police custody during his honeymoon.
The Diplomat (Aug 2026): Indonesia's transgender community faces growing repression - vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions.

PAK.name: Pakistan
PAK.summary:
Pakistan is high-risk — legally progressive on paper but severely undermined in practice. The 2018 Transgender Persons Protection Act was "one of the most progressive internationally" (third-gender recognition since 2009), but the Federal Shariat Court gutted it in 2023 (declaring provisions "un-Islamic"). Transgender people face extreme violence: three trans women were shot dead in Karachi (bodies on a roadside), 267 violence cases were documented in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and police commit a documented "continuum of violence — from routine harassment to arbitrary detention, extortion, and abuse in custody." The jirga (tribal) system closes cases under family pressure.

Same-sex conduct is NOT clearly criminalised nationally (the Zina Ordinance is unclear; no known cases or executions), and there is no Sharia cross-dressing criminalisation (unlike Malaysia). No trans-traveler-specific border friction or death in custody is documented (unlike the UAE or Indonesia). But the severity of social and police violence is extreme.

Pakistan has a significant hijra/third-gender community with some legal recognition, and civil society is active (a dedicated ride-sharing service for trans safety launched in Lahore, and activists are appealing the Shariat Court ruling to the Supreme Court).
PAK.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism risks, sectarian violence, and general crime in certain regions affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: NOTE: Page content did not load at fetch time (only AP site navigation was retrieved); the underlying article covers transgender women killed in Karachi.

BBC (Sept 2025): the bodies of three transgender people, shot dead, were found on a roadside in Karachi's Memon Goth area - the latest violence against a community of an estimated half a million trans citizens facing social exclusion and abuse; Amnesty notes a concerning rise in violence; the 2018 Transgender Rights Act's key sections were later revoked by a sharia court.

Justice Project Pakistan policy brief (April 2026): 'Preventing Torture Against Transgender Persons in Pakistan' - trans people face a continuum of violence from law enforcement (harassment, arbitrary detention, extortion, custodial abuse); the challenge is not absence of legal protections but failure of implementation - no binding operational frameworks, independent oversight or accessible complaint mechanisms.
UK Home Office CPIN Pakistan: sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (Nov 2025, updated July 2026): official country-of-origin information and assessment for asylum claims.

Amnesty International (May 2023): responding to the Federal Shariat Court's reserved verdict striking down sections of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 - 'a blow to the rights of the already beleaguered group'; some court observations were based on presumptive scenarios rather than empirical evidence.

The News (Oct 2025): 'Between legal rights and lived realities' - despite the 2018 Act, trans Pakistanis face violence, harassment, landlord rejection and hospital/police apathy; in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa alone 267 cases of violence over five years with only one conviction; traces the legal history from the Criminal Tribes Act 1871 through the 2011 Supreme Court recognition, the 2018 Act, the 2020 'X' marker rules, and the 2023 FSC strike-down of self-identification.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Feb 2026): anti-trans officials and violence reverse progress for transgender Pakistanis - Senator Mushtaq Ahmad proposes a government 'gender re-assignment board' controlling official gender identity; a wave of violence (shootings at activists' homes) has left trans people afraid to go out; the 2023 shariat court ruling undercut the 2018 law.

Dawn (May 2023) by Nayyab Ali: 'Westernised transgenders or colonised transphobes?' - examines the FSC verdict on the Transgender Rights Act; the petitioners' concerns echo right-wing Western anti-trans narratives; describes the 2018 Act's protections (anti-discrimination, welfare, offences against trans people).

The Diplomat (July 2025): Pakistan's transgender citizens - legally recognized, socially forsaken; for 500,000 trans Pakistanis, constitutional rights remain hollow in the face of violence and exclusion.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Pakistan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under Section 377; societal violence and discrimination; transgender persons (khwaja sira) have some legal recognition but face harassment and violence.

PAK.localsOnly: The 2018 Act's third-gender recognition (gutted by the Shariat Court in 2023, under appeal) and the hijra community's legal recognition are resident-facing; the 267 documented KP violence cases and jirga case-closures describe residents' situation.
PAK.blindSummary:
For trans visitors there is a stark gap between law and practice here: the formal framework is progressive on paper but severely undermined in reality. A 2018 transgender-protection act was called "one of the most progressive internationally" (third-gender recognition has existed since 2009), but a federal religious court gutted it in 2023, declaring key provisions contrary to religious law. Transgender people face extreme violence: three trans women were shot dead and left on a roadside in the largest city, 267 violence cases were documented in one province, and police commit a "continuum of violence — from routine harassment to arbitrary detention, extortion, and abuse in custody." A tribal-council justice system closes cases under family pressure.

Same-sex conduct is NOT clearly criminalised nationally (a religious-morality ordinance is unclear; no known cases or executions), and there is no religious-law criminalisation of cross-dressing. No trans-traveller-specific border friction or death in custody is documented. But the severity of social and police violence is extreme.

The country has a large indigenous third-gender community with some legal recognition, and civil society is active (a dedicated ride-sharing service for trans safety launched in a major city, and activists are appealing the religious-court ruling to the country's top court).
PAK.blindOutOfScope: Terrorism risks, sectarian violence, and general crime in certain areas affect all travellers; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.

PHL.name: Philippines
PHL.summary:
The Philippines is one of Asia's most socially accepting destinations for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity (bakla, tomboy), a vibrant Manila Pride, and no criminalisation. Trans identity has never been criminalised.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (trans people cannot change their gender marker), the SOGIE Equality Bill has been stalled for 25 years (no national anti-discrimination law), and documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a Chinese national arrested for raping a transwoman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The Commission on Human Rights actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction, social acceptance is genuine, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue (documented incidents of bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials).
PHL.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (kidnapping risks in certain provinces, scams, typhoon risks) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

CHL.name: Chile
CHL.summary:
Chile has a strong legal framework — a gender identity law allowing self-determination (2019, no medical requirements), marriage equality (2022), a hate-crime law covering gender identity (2012), and a positive Gendarmería protocol that places trans inmates in facilities matching their gender identity and provides healthcare examination (better than most European countries on axis-H). The UN Human Rights Committee commended Chile's police measures to promote LGBTIQ rights.

But 2024 was a "year of regression" (the first rollback since democracy returned in 1990), with lawmakers rejecting nondiscrimination-law reforms and a 2025 Movilh report describing a "breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus" on LGBTIQ+ rights. Documented violence includes a trans person murdered and dismembered ("the biggest hate crime in Chile"), a transphobic hotel attack in Santiago (beating, captivity, death threats), and institutional discrimination against Chile's first trans police officer.

The Supreme Court restored a femicide conviction for the murder of a trans woman (overturning an appeals-court ruling that she didn't "legally qualify" as a woman). For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Santiago is welcoming.
CHL.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (theft, scams) and earthquake risk affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

COL.name: Colombia
COL.summary:
Colombia has one of Latin America's strongest legal frameworks — Constitutional Court legal gender recognition since 1993 (no surgery required, based on self-recognition), "trans" and "non-binary" ID markers (November 2025), a Comprehensive Trans Law being legislated (2025), marriage equality (2016), and a Constitutional Court ruling protecting a trans inmate from prison violence. President Petro's government is pro-LGBTIQ+.

But the law-versus-practice gap is extreme and violent. More than 40 trans women were killed in a single year, with armed groups running "social cleansing" campaigns (Caquetá) and posting kill-lists targeting specific LGBTQ individuals ("All will be military targets"). Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was tortured and murdered in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, with a viral video of the assault. The UN Independent Expert urged Colombia to "close the gap between laws and lived realities amid rising violence."

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Bogotá's Chapinero district is a well-established LGBTQ+ area. The armed-group violence is concentrated in conflict regions and targets local communities, not tourists — but the organized targeting is a distinctive, severe concern.
COL.outOfScopeNotes: The US State Department advises reconsidering travel to Colombia due to crime, terrorism, and kidnapping risks; these affect all travellers.

NGA.name: Nigeria
NGA.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this a Do Not Travel environment.
NGA.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (Boko Haram in the northeast), kidnapping, and violent crime affect all travellers in many regions; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

The Dial (Feb 2025): 'Threats, Raids and Potlucks' - reporting on what it's like to be queer in Nigeria, centred on Abuja Area Mama's killing; six months later no suspects charged; the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation; transphobia and homophobia are common with no legal protections.

KEN.name: Kenya
KEN.summary:
Kenya is high-risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the colonial-era Penal Code (14 years, applies to all including tourists). Police extortion targeting trans people is documented and systemic — a trans woman was forced to pay a $50 bribe in Mombasa, and 25 trans and intersex people told CNN this kind of police harassment is "common." The Kenya Human Rights Commission's "Lives on the Line" report documented 102 evictions, 43 unlawful arrests, and mob violence (groups stripping queer people naked) over a one-year period. An LGBTQ+ activist, Edwin Chiloba, was murdered (his body found in a metal box) — though the perpetrator was sentenced to 50 years, showing enforcement can work.

However, Kenya's courts have been a surprising bright spot. The High Court ruled in 2025 that a trans woman's arrest for "personation" was unconstitutional (awarding damages and ordering the government to draft a Transgender Protection Rights Bill). In May 2026, the High Court affirmed a constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court has upheld LGBTQ+ freedom of association, and the Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional. "Thousands of gay travelers visit annually through specialized tour operators."

There is no anti-discrimination law and no LGR procedure yet, but the court-ordered Transgender Protection Rights Bill is a positive trajectory.
KEN.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism risks near the Somali border, general crime, and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

ROU.name: Romania
ROU.summary:
Romania is reduced-risk with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark EU court ruling and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Romania must recognize gender-identity changes made in other EU member states (the Mirin case), and a Romanian court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. Bucharest Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the Orthodox Church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

For a visitor: EU/Schengen, no trans-specific border friction, no criminalisation, bathrooms unrestricted. The ECJ ruling means EU-issued LGR documents must be recognised.
ROU.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is moderate.

BGD.name: Bangladesh
BGD.summary:
Bangladesh is high-risk for trans visitors, with escalating Islamist violence since the August 2024 political crisis that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having "skyrocketed." Islamist fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been "forced into hiding." A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (one survivor said "I escaped only with my life").

Police extort hijra/trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at Dhaka's international airport.

The US State Department rates Bangladesh as Level 3 (Reconsider Travel).
BGD.outOfScopeNotes: Political instability, mob violence/lynchings, terrorism, and cyclone/monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

VNM.name: Vietnam
VNM.summary:
Vietnam is reduced-risk — described as "one of Asia's most tolerant countries toward sexual minorities." Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the Civil Code (2015, Article 37) was a landmark that recognised transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the implementing Gender Affirmation Law has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented (unlike several neighbours), but conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma, lack of trans-competent providers, and "red tape" in accessing care. In September 2025, Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and five LGBTQ events, shocking activists (though Hanoi's Pride proceeded).

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, and no criminalisation. But Vietnam is a one-party authoritarian state where "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice" (Amnesty), and the stalled LGR means no practical gender-marker change. The UN Development Programme is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies.
VNM.outOfScopeNotes: One-party state political controls, arbitrary detention of dissidents, and typhoon/monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

UGA.name: Uganda
UGA.summary:
Uganda is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act imposes life imprisonment for same-sex conduct and the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality," and the US State Department explicitly warns that "the law applies to both visitors and residents." Over 1,000 rights violations (arrests, torture, evictions) were documented in nine months. Mobs have gathered outside trans people's homes (one woman described being grabbed and shouted at that she needed to die); police use digital entrapment (obtaining evidence via dating apps); and the government has "spread misinformation and hatred against LGBT people." The law also criminalises the "promotion of homosexuality," meaning any advocacy or support is banned.

There are no laws regulating gender identity — the AHA targets same-sex conduct and promotion, not trans identity per se — but trans people are swept up in the broader anti-LGBT crackdown, mobs, and state violence. The Constitutional Court upheld the AHA in April 2024 (striking down only a few provisions on healthcare access and renting).

Uganda's death penalty is for "aggravated" same-sex (not all same-sex like Iran; not gender expression per se like Saudi), and no trans-specific visitor killing or border-targeting is documented — but the systematic state-led crackdown makes this a Do Not Travel environment.
UGA.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (ADF in border areas), violent crime (armed robbery, sexual assault), and civil unrest affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

EGY.name: Egypt
EGY.summary:
Egypt is high-risk for trans visitors — with a directly documented study on the treatment of queer foreigners by Egyptian authorities ("Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here," Cairo 52, 12 incidents 2018-2022). Same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalised, but authorities use "debauchery" and cybercrime laws (six months + fine for "violation of social and family values") to arrest and prosecute — and courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation under the cybercrime law.

Police hunt LGBT people on dating apps (BBC Grindr entrapment) and subject arrestees to coerced anal examinations. Gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited. The Ministry of Interior is closing a loophole that allowed limited legal gender recognition. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity in its 2025 Universal Periodic Review. The authorities' approach is described as "not only to criminalize LGBTQ+ identities but also to erase them from society and public life."

Egypt has no death penalty for same-sex (unlike Uganda/Nigeria's death penalties), no documented trans-specific tourist killing, and the statutory penalty is six months + fine (not 14 years or life) — but the systematic police entrapment, foreigner-targeting, coerced anal exams, and healthcare prohibition make the practical risk severe.
EGY.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (Sinai), political instability, and general crime affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 report 'Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here' (Nov 2023) on Egypt's treatment of queer foreigners: analysis of immigration law and 12 incidents (2018-2022). The Ministry of Interior has broad powers to deport or deny entry to anyone 'disturbing public order and morality', interpreted to allow denial of entry and deportation of people perceived as queer; transgender and gender-nonconforming people are most vulnerable to being denied entry.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): no explicit criminalisation but vague public-morality and 'debauchery' laws used for arrests and prison sentences; dating apps (e.g. Grindr) used for entrapment, with condoms or cash used as evidence of 'habitual debauchery'; the 2018 cybercrime law penalises online content 'threatening family values'; no SOGISC discrimination protection; no legal gender recognition and no functioning pathway to gender-affirming healthcare.

PER.name: Peru
PER.summary:
Peru is elevated-risk with a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence against trans people, but no criminalisation of trans identity and an unprecedented 17-year conviction for police torture of a trans woman. Congress approved (February-April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated axis-C restriction comparable to US state bans or the UK EHRC code. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 TLGBI people were assassinated (trans women most affected). In the Azul Rojas Marín case, three police officers were sentenced to 17 years for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman (December 2025) — an unprecedented conviction for Peru and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. A presidential decree briefly classified trans identity as a "mental disorder" (May 2024), but was walked back after massive protests.

For a visitor: no border friction, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure when using public facilities.
PER.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (theft, robbery) and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

URY.name: Uruguay
URY.summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming.
URY.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is very low; no trans-specific travel advisory.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): broad protections - same-sex marriage since 2013, adoption since 2009, accessible legal gender recognition; since 2021 more than 120 trans people have accessed a reparation pension for institutional violence suffered during the 1973-1985 dictatorship; anti-discrimination law explicitly covers SOGI and hate-crime laws include SOGI aggravating circumstances.

Cornell Law School resource on Uruguay's Ley N° 19684 (2018), the Comprehensive Law for Trans People: ensures the right to a life free of discrimination and stigmatisation; the right to free development of personality per one's gender identity regardless of biological/genetic/anatomical factors; right to identification matching gender identity; includes reparation mechanisms.

Equaldex data for Montevideo (governed by federal Uruguay law): homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, gender-affirming care legal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected.

Uruguayan Presidency (Nov 2018, in Spanish): the Executive promulgated the Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons (Law 19,684) - the right to gender identity and a life free of discrimination, name/sex change on identity documents, and a reparation regime for trans people born before 31 December 1975 who suffered institutional violence or deprivation of liberty.

Freedom House 2024 for Uruguay: 'Free' (96/100) - historically strong democratic governance; disparities remain in treatment and political representation of women, transgender people, Afro-Uruguayans and the Indigenous population.

Trans Lives Matter / TDoR memorial entry (July 2025): Joana, 29, a trans woman shot in the head at her home in Montevideo's Bella Italia neighbourhood; police hypothesised the attack targeted the man with her and she was a collateral victim; the perpetrator was sentenced to 7 years; the state expressed sorrow.

PinkNews (Dec 2007): Uruguay became the first Latin American country to recognise same-sex civil unions - President Tabare Vazquez signed the law granting cohabiting couples (5+ years) the same rights as married couples, 'of any sex, identity, orientation or sexual option'; the Episcopal Conference of Uruguay attacked the validity of gay relationships.

QAT.name: Qatar
QAT.summary:
Qatar is Do Not Travel for trans visitors, with the most severe documented police practice in the Gulf. Human Rights Watch interviewed four transgender women arrested by the Preventive Security Department between 2019 and 2022 based solely on their gender expression in public places. One was arrested for wearing makeup — officers made her wipe it off, used the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her, and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All described sexual harassment in custody, forced phone-unlocking to identify other LGBT people, and mandatory conversion-therapy sessions as a condition of release. Detention was in an underground prison in Doha; one woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and physical detransition (forced breast-tissue removal) was reported.

No statute has been repealed: trans people are arrested for "impersonating the opposite gender" and "violating public morality" under community-protection laws allowing up to 6 months' detention without charge or trial. Arrests continued even during the 2022 World Cup under international scrutiny.
QAT.outOfScopeNotes: Migrant-worker abuses, kafala labour system, and general human-rights concerns affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

KWT.name: Kuwait
KWT.summary:
Kuwait is High Risk — the least hostile of the Gulf states, but not safe. In 2007, Article 198 of the Penal Code criminalised "imitating the opposite sex in any way" (up to 1 year in jail); within two weeks at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, coffee shops, and taxis, three were beaten (one into unconsciousness), and heads were shaved as punishment. HRW's 2012 report "They Hunt Us Down for Fun" documented police violence against trans women under this law.

However, in February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck down Article 198 as unconstitutional — the only Gulf state to repeal its cross-dressing statute. The repeal has teeth: a cisgender woman arrested over a short haircut won 4,000 KWD in compensation, with the Court of Cassation ruling police had arrested her "without justification." Being visibly trans is no longer a crime in Kuwait.

But the repeal is incomplete in practice: HRW reports transgender people "continue to face threats and harassment," and in December 2022 security forces carried out mass deportations of LGBT people under "security" measures. For a trans traveler: no criminal exposure for gender expression itself, courts now provide recourse, but police harassment and deportation risk remain real.
KWT.outOfScopeNotes: Migrant-worker labour conditions affect all foreign workers; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

BHR.name: Bahrain
BHR.summary:
Bahrain is Do Not Travel, but with the thinnest active-enforcement record in the Gulf. Uniquely among Gulf states, same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1976, and there is no statute criminalising transgender expression. The UK foreign office notes "arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare."

However, broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions are used against gender and sexual minorities — penalties include imprisonment, fines, and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a Manama hotel discotheque on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A Brazilian trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite a female passport marker. In 2023 a court rejected a trans man's recognition application citing Islamic Sharia, and in February 2024 the lower house of parliament adopted a bill to criminalise "acts of deviance" — a deteriorating trajectory.

For a visitor: the legal exposure is real but enforcement is sporadic; the modal risk is indecency arrest followed by deportation rather than imprisonment.
BHR.outOfScopeNotes: Political repression, restrictions on free expression, and labour concerns affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

The court cited Sharia to deny both healthcare and recognition.

Laws are used to punish gender non-conformity; discriminatory violence by state and non-state actors is widely reported; trans people are denied gender-affirming healthcare (intersex people are permitted medical transition).

No LGBTIQ organisations operate; a 2023 court denied a trans man's gender-marker change, echoing a 2016 ruling.

OMN.name: Oman
OMN.summary:
Oman is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — and uniquely in the Gulf, combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveler abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, extending to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the Royal Oman Police publicly announced arresting transgender women in Salalah after private-party photos circulated on social media; HRW documented arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travelers: in February 2024, Nin Kala, an Indian non-binary model and designer arriving at Muscat airport on a tourist visa, was pulled aside while their friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. Kala warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these Gulf countries."
OMN.outOfScopeNotes: Political restrictions and labour conditions affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

BGR.name: Bulgaria
BGR.summary:
Bulgaria is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — an EU member with no traveler-facing restrictions, but one of the EU's most hostile social climates. There is no bathroom law, no border friction for foreign passports, and no criminalisation of gender expression. The European Court of Justice is actively hearing the Shipov case on Bulgaria's refusal to issue ID matching lived gender, and EU free-movement law provides a legal backstop.

The concerns are climate rather than traveler law: the Supreme Court of Cassation ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible (gender an "unchangeable biological factor"), parliament passed a Russia-style law banning "propaganda" of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools (August 2024), and the EU's FRA survey finds 75% of LGBTIQ people in Bulgaria avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault — both far above EU averages. Hate speech by politicians is routine.

For a visitor: document mismatch carries no legal penalty, police do not target trans expression, and Sofia has a small but visible scene. The risk is street hostility if read as trans — verbal harassment is common, physical assault possible but not systematic.
BGR.outOfScopeNotes: Roma minority issues and asylum-system abuses are out of scope.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Bulgaria: in August 2024 a law banning representation of LGBTI identities in schools was introduced (spearheaded by Vazrazhdane leader Kostadinov); Bulgaria continues rejecting asylum requests by LGBTI people from Russia and Belarus and unlawfully detains LGBTI asylum-seekers from Palestine in closed detention; a Sofia Pride performer received death threats; a LGBTI youth organisation faced institutional checks.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004, expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex change' under 'sex'. But Article 46 of the constitution bans same-sex marriage, and there is no legal gender recognition. Koilova and Babulkova v. Bulgaria (ECtHR 2023) found Bulgaria in violation of its obligations on non-recognition of same-sex relationships.

EU FRA LGBTIQ survey III country sheet for Bulgaria (2024): 75% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (EU-27: 53%); 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (EU-27: 29%); only 27% are open about being LGBTIQ (EU-27: 51%); 28% felt discriminated against at work or looking for work. Indicates a strongly hostile day-to-day climate.

DW (Sept 2025): ECJ Advocate General Richard de la Tour issued a non-binding opinion that Bulgaria must not refuse a trans woman ID documents matching her presented sex ('lived gender identity') - the Shipov case, concerning a Bulgarian trans woman on hormone therapy refused documents; such opinions are followed by the Court in roughly two-thirds of cases.

Strasbourg Observers analysis (Dec 2024) of Y.T. v. Bulgaria: the original 2020 ECtHR judgment found an Article 8 violation over refusal of legal gender recognition; on revision (July 2024) the application was declared inadmissible for abuse of rights, but the Court confirmed Bulgaria remains obliged under Article 8 (per P.H. v. Bulgaria) to provide a framework for legal gender recognition - which Bulgaria still lacks.

Amnesty International report (Feb 2015): 'Missing the point' - Bulgaria's failure to adequately investigate and prosecute hate crimes fuels fear, discrimination and violence against asylum seekers, migrants, Muslims and LGBT people; authorities consistently fail to identify bias motivation.

BGR.blindSummary:
This country is a member of a regional union with no traveler-facing restrictions on trans visitors, but one of the most hostile social climates inside that union. There is no bathroom law, no border friction for foreign passports, and no criminalisation of gender expression. The union's court of justice is actively hearing a case on this country's refusal to issue ID documents matching a person's lived gender, and the union's free-movement law provides a legal backstop.

The concerns are climate rather than traveler law: the supreme court ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible (characterising gender as an unchangeable biological fact); parliament passed an August 2024 law, modelled on a similar foreign statute, banning school-level "propaganda" of non-traditional sexual orientation; and a regional rights-agency survey finds 75% of LGBTIQ people here avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault — both far above the union-wide averages (53% and 29%). Hate speech by politicians is routine.

For a visitor: document mismatch carries no legal penalty, police do not target trans expression, and the capital has a small but visible scene. The risk is street hostility if read as trans — verbal harassment is common, physical assault possible but not systematic.
BGR.blindOutOfScope: Ethnic-minority issues and asylum-system abuses are out of scope.

SVK.name: Slovakia
SVK.summary:
Slovakia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. There are no traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues, EU free movement, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events.

The climate is the concern. In October 2022, a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside Tepláreň, a Bratislava LGBT bar — classified as Slovakia's first modern terrorist attack. The state responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding: parliament advanced a bill to make legal gender recognition impossible (genetic-test-only basis), and constitutional amendments declaring gender immutable have been proposed. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in Bratislava.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, but elevated risk of street hostility and a political trajectory moving against trans recognition.
SVK.outOfScopeNotes: The LGR-ban bill and constitutional gender amendments are resident-facing climate signals. Roma discrimination is out of scope.

BLR.name: Belarus
BLR.summary:
Belarus is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. In 2024 the authorities escalated from hostility to active persecution: a Culture Ministry decree reclassified transgender identity itself — "the desire to live and be seen by others as a person of an opposite sex" — as pornography, punishable by up to four years in prison. In September 2024 a wave of arrests targeted the community: TG House Belarus documented over 15 LGBTQ+ people detained, including at least eight transgender people, several arrested for merely subscribing to "extremist" resources online.

Detained trans people were beaten and forced to record humiliating "confession videos" circulated on pro-government channels. ODIHR's 2024 reporting notes the majority of bias incidents in Belarus targeted trans people, including "physical assaults, threats, abductions, humiliation, and coerced confessions related to their gender identity by law enforcement officers." State media runs systematic dehumanising propaganda.

Gender transition technically remains legal, but the 2024 pornography decree means a discoverable online presence or simply living visibly as trans can be prosecuted. For a visitor: no documented trans-tourist case yet, but police actively hunt trans people, any visible gender nonconformity risks detention, and foreign nationals receive no protection.
BLR.outOfScopeNotes: General political repression and the post-2020 protest crackdown affect everyone; the score reflects trans-specific risk.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.summary:
Ukraine is Reduced Risk for trans visitors, with the caveat that this scores trans-specific risk, not the obvious general risks of an active war zone. Ukraine criminalises nothing about being trans; legal gender recognition exists (medicalised — a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation under the 2016 protocol), and a resilient civil society (Gender Stream, Insight) operates openly. Kyiv hosted a three-day Trans Forum in June 2026 even during the war.

Trans-specific frictions exist but mostly affect residents, not visitors: trans women with male passports cannot leave the country under martial law (conscription), and wartime document checks can out people. A foreign visitor's passport is not subject to mobilisation rules, so border crossing is governed by standard wartime entry rules. There is no SOGI-specific hate-crime law, societal attitudes lag EU averages, and the healthcare system is war-disrupted (hormone shortages, diagnostic corruption reported).

Ukraine scores far above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) — no criminalisation, no state persecution, functioning NGOs — and below Serbia (0.64) and Moldova (0.65), reflecting wartime institutional strain and weaker legal protections rather than active hostility.
UKR.outOfScopeNotes: General war risks (missile strikes, infrastructure, mobilisation) apply to all travelers and are out of scope for the trans-specific score. Trans residents' draft exposure is noted as context but does not govern the visitor score.

MDA.name: Moldova
MDA.summary:
Moldova is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — the best-protected of the former-Soviet states outside the Baltics. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity, and Chisinau Pride marches through the city centre under police protection. Moldova is on the EU accession path, driving continued legal alignment.

Counterweights: there is still no accessible legal gender recognition (a medicalised process exists on paper but Genderdoc-M reports it is not functional in practice), the Orthodox Church and major politicians (including Chisinau's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements, and the breakaway Russian-controlled region of Transnistria has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travelers should treat Transnistria as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.
MDA.outOfScopeNotes: Transnistria is scored as part of Moldova de jure but travelers should treat it separately: Russian-controlled, anti-LGBT propaganda law, no consular access. General poverty and corruption affect all travelers.

Amnesty International Moldova report 2025: discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace; freedom of expression and assembly arbitrarily restricted; in Russian-occupied Transnistria new legislation prohibits 'promotion of non-traditional sexual relations'.

GENDERDOC-M report on the situation of LGBT+ rights in Moldova (2023): the Equality Council's 2022 study found extremely low acceptance - 79% of the population would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues; social distance score 5.7; marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased in 2022 amid pandemic, economic and security crises.
Attitude (Feb 2026): revisits Moldova Pride 2024 - a country slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity; participants of all ages and backgrounds join the festivities.

MDA.comparisons: Moldova scores below Romania (0.67 — functional LGR, EU member longer) and above Serbia (0.64 — comparable climate but Moldova's 2022 SOGI hate-crime law and EU-candidate trajectory give it the edge) and Ukraine (0.62 — war strain).

LUX.name: Luxembourg
LUX.summary:
Luxembourg is Low Risk — one of Europe's strongest trans jurisdictions. AND.name: Andorra

ILGA-Europe records only three bias-motivated incidents in the most recent annual review — a tiny absolute number reflecting a small, safe, tourism-dependent country.

No traveler-facing concerns: no bathroom laws, no border issues (open border with Spain/France, though outside Schengen there are no document-gender checks), high social tolerance in practice despite a conservative Catholic history. MCO.name: Monaco

Monaco is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. There is no functioning legal gender recognition process (ILGA-Europe lists Monaco among states without one), but that is a resident-facing gap: a visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever. Monaco is a tiny, heavily-policed, very low-crime tourist enclave embedded in France; street violence of any kind is rare.

No bathroom laws, no border friction (entry via France, Schengen rules), no documented anti-trans incidents. The score reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness (no LGR, limited explicit trans protections).

VAT.name: Vatican City
VAT.summary:
Vatican City is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — and an unusual case: it is a 0.49 km² tourist enclave (museums, basilica, square) with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathrooms inspections, no morality police, and the Swiss Guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile: the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and there is obviously no legal recognition or protection of any kind. But this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism — the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

CYP.name: Cyprus
CYP.summary:
Cyprus is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. The legal framework is mid-transition: public incitement to hatred based on gender identity is a criminal offence (2015), and gender identity is an aggravating factor in hate crime (2017). A legal gender recognition bill (self-determination basis) was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and is pending in parliament; until it passes, LGR requires surgery under the 2002 Civil Registry Law — a resident-facing gap.

No traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues (EU member), tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to diverse visitors. Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the non-discrimination framework, and the divided island matters: the northern part (de facto Turkish-controlled) has its own LGR regime requiring surgical proof, weaker protections, and less documentation — travelers should treat the north as closer to Turkey's risk profile.
CYP.outOfScopeNotes: The north/south division and pending LGR bill are noted; LGR requirements are resident-facing.

KHM.name: Cambodia
KHM.summary:
Cambodia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: the Cambodian Centre for Human Rights documents “shocking” harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported Siem Reap police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially.
KHM.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and discrimination-law gaps are resident-facing.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex activity, but Article 45 of the constitution defines marriage as between one husband and one wife; at its 2024 UPR Cambodia accepted all 12 LGBTIQ recommendations including seven toward marriage equality; no SOGISC discrimination protections; a 2018 two-men wedding ceremony in Kratie was interrupted by authorities.

NPL.name: Nepal
NPL.summary:
Nepal is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — South Asia's most legally recognising country. The Supreme Court has protected gender identity since the landmark 2007 Sunil Babu Pant decision; a third-gender “O” category exists on documents by self-identification; and in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled (Rukshana Kapali case) that a trans woman must be recognised as female without medical verification. Nothing is criminalised, and Kathmandu has an established activist scene (Blue Diamond Society, founded 2001).

The gap between doctrine and practice is large: HRW documents (“We Have to Beg So Many People,” 2024) that implementation is piecemeal and humiliating, and trans people in provinces like Madhesh face physical and sexual harassment in public spaces with little police protection. These burdens fall overwhelmingly on residents navigating citizenship documents — a visitor with a foreign passport faces none of the bureaucratic gauntlet.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, tolerant tourist areas, but expect stares and possible harassment if visibly trans outside Kathmandu/Pokhara bubbles.
NPL.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation barriers are resident-facing; citizenship-law discrimination does not affect visitors.

sources.summary: NOTE: Page content did not load at fetch time (only HRW site navigation was retrieved); the underlying Feb 2024 piece covers barriers to transgender legal recognition in Nepal.

Context: 'other'/third-gender categories exist since a 2007 ruling, but changing markers to male/female usually requires surgery abroad plus intrusive post-operative genital exams.

The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's trans-rights reputation needs to be matched with real policy - the country's LGBTIQ+ rights record is more complicated than it first appears; progressive reputation vs implementation gaps.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024): the complexity of transgender life in Janakpur - nine trans people sharing a flat; discrimination in public spaces and government institutions, physical and sexual harassment; celebrated as entertainers but objectified and ridiculed.
