LKA.name: Sri Lanka
LKA.summary:
Sri Lanka is High Risk for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.
LKA.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; LGR circular limits are resident-facing.

Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).

MNG.name: Mongolia
MNG.summary:
Mongolia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and SOGI was added to the hate-crime provisions of the Criminal Code in 2015. Legal gender recognition exists via a medicalised process, and Ulaanbaatar has an organised community (LGBT Centre) that successfully lobbied for these protections.

Counterweights: protections are fragmented (no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering all areas), the LGBT Centre has documented periods of elevated hate speech and assaults — including attacks on its own staff — and social acceptance outside the capital is low. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; the realistic risk is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside central Ulaanbaatar.
MNG.outOfScopeNotes: Comprehensive anti-discrimination gaps and medicalised LGR are resident-facing.

MMR.name: Myanmar
MMR.summary:
Myanmar is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Section 377 of the Penal Code criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use “shadow laws” — notably Section 30(d) of the Rangoon Police Act, allowing detention of anyone who cannot “satisfactorily account” for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: the National Unity Government documented 17 LGBT people killed by mid-2022, and rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities, with the 2024 Conscription Law falling brutally on queer people.

In 2025 the junta banned seven books for LGBTQ+ content as “obscene.” There is no legal gender recognition, no protection of any kind, and no institutional recourse — police and military are the primary predators. Resistance-controlled areas are nominally friendlier but are active war zones.

For a visitor: any visible gender nonconformity risks detention under police-act powers, with torture documented in custody; the general security collapse compounds everything.
MMR.outOfScopeNotes: General civil-war risks affect all travelers and are out of scope; the score reflects trans-specific persecution by the junta.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Section 377 criminalises same-sex intimacy, reinforced by 'shadow laws' and police discretion (e.g. Section 30(d) of the 1899 Rangoon Police Act used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence). Since the February 2021 coup, risks have intensified sharply - abuses in interrogation and detention reflecting homophobia, transphobia and punitive sexual violence; the UN Special Rapporteur warns of widespread sexual and gender-based violence against women, girls and LGBTQ people.

DVB (Jan 2024): LGBT discrimination on the rise since the 2021 coup - attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse by authorities; the NUG Ministry of Human Rights stated 17 LGBT people were killed and two critically injured since Feb 2021; first-person accounts from trans women protesters.

Human Rights Myanmar submission (June 2024) to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions: killing of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled Myanmar - 5 to 12 individuals dead since the coup; Section 377 enforcement intensified as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

RFA (Jan 2025): Myanmar's junta banned seven books with LGBTQ+ themes and will take legal action against their publishers, calling them 'obscene' and socially unacceptable - part of the community's long oppression in conservative Myanmar.

A historic penal-code provision criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use "shadow laws" — notably a provision of an 1899 municipal police law allowing detention of anyone who cannot "satisfactorily account" for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: the opposition government-in-exile has documented 17 LGBT people killed by mid-2022, and rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by the military government's forces, with the 2024 conscription law falling brutally on queer people.

CUB.name: Cuba
CUB.summary:
Cuba is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — one of Latin America's most legally transformed countries. The 2019 Constitution bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the 2022 Family Code (66.87% referendum approval) overhauled family law; and trans people can change legal gender — the July 2025 civil-registry reform further eliminated bureaucratic hurdles for name changes. CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme, and Havana has a visible, state-tolerated trans community.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific: Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, the economic crisis has degraded healthcare (hormone availability is unreliable), and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people as trans — the historical UMAP camps era is long past and officially repudiated — but there is also no independent recourse if something goes wrong.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression or documents; low street-hostility in tourist areas; the risk is the general absence of rule-of-law recourse.
CUB.outOfScopeNotes: Political repression, shortages, and detention powers affect all travelers; LGR mechanics are resident-facing.

ECU.name: Ecuador
ECU.summary:
Ecuador is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — a country whose legal framework is now among Latin America's strongest while its streets are among the region's most dangerous. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016; the 2024 Organic Law reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the ID card directly through the Civil Registry (one time, no surgery); and in 2024-25 Constitutional Court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the Assembly for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: Runa Sipiy documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023, with inadequate state response, and the “internal armed conflict” against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024 — two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks. Quito and Guayaquil carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis.

For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in South America right now.
ECU.outOfScopeNotes: The general security emergency affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific legal/violence balance.

JAM.name: Jamaica
JAM.summary:
Jamaica is High Risk for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.
JAM.outOfScopeNotes: The buggery law is a situational/climate factor; resort vs. non-resort risk differs sharply.

TTO.name: Trinidad and Tobago
TTO.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.
TTO.outOfScopeNotes: Decriminalisation status and reform rejections are climate/legal context; no trans-specific statute exists.

sources.summary: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday (July 2024): 'Long way yet for recognition, safe spaces' - TT Transgender Coalition director Rae Alibey says the trans community is the most marginalised and not even recognised in T&T; gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation; gender-identity markers on institutional forms are absent; national discussions and attitudinal research needed.

Newsday (Nov 2024): police warning over cyber criminals - Grindr hook-ups ending in cars, cash and phones stolen; criminals create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault; two separate incidents reported in one week.

Newsday editorial (June 2024): 'Grind hate to a halt' - a spate of Grindr-related attacks (almost half a dozen in recent months); Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne points to gaps in the law: 'We don't have a specific hate crime category in legislation'; the editorial argues the gap must be closed.

CNC3 (Aug 2024): CAISO head unhappy LGBTQ rights reform ignored again - the PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected reform of sexual-orientation rights; CAISO had recommended adding sexual orientation and gender identity to protected statuses under section 4 of the Constitution; 'no political party has stepped up'.

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Trinidad & Tobago' (Aug 2012): although homosexuality is illegal, 'the laws are mostly ignored' - context of the islands' history from Spanish colonisation through British rule.

PinkNews (Nov 2017) by Jason Jones: 'I am a criminal simply because I am a gay man' - his High Court challenge to Trinidad and Tobago's laws (up to 25 years for 'serious indecency'); ~100,000 LGBT people live under the threat; the laws were inherited from Britain but extended to lesbians after independence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (June 2016): PM Keith Rowley claimed the state must protect all citizens 'regardless of whom they sleep with', but said there were no plans to amend the buggery laws and declined to address the EOC's call for anti-discrimination protection.

GHA.name: Ghana
GHA.summary:
Ghana is High Risk for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” President Akufo-Addo refused to assent pending legal challenges, the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. Accra has a resilient underground community (LGBT+ Rights Ghana — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.
GHA.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 bill never became law (lapsed unassented); its significance is climate/trajectory.

NOTE: Page content did not load at fetch time (only HRW site navigation was retrieved); the underlying March 2024 piece calls on Ghana's president to veto the anti-LGBT bill.

BBC (Dec 2024): Ghana's Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two legal challenges to the anti-LGBT bill (three years' imprisonment for identifying as LGBT, five for forming or funding LGBT groups), ruling the cases could not be reviewed until presidential assent. Gay sex was already punishable by up to three years. Fear and uncertainty gripped Ghana's LGBT community; the UN condemned the bill as one of Africa's most draconian.

JURIST (Feb 2024): Ghana's Parliament unanimously passed the Promotion of Proper Human Sexual Rights and Ghanaian Family Values Bill 2021, criminalising identifying as LGBTQ+ (up to 3 years) and forming or funding LGBT groups (up to 5 years); the bill proscribes 'propaganda, advocacy or promotion' of LGBTQ+ activities.

HRW report (Jan 2018) 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am': full PDF - violence and discrimination against LGBT people in Ghana; section 104(1)(b) criminalises 'unnatural carnal knowledge' but is rarely enforced; documents mob violence, police abuse, and extortion.

HRW report page (Jan 2018): opens with Pearl's account - a lesbian woman beaten by a crowd and nearly burned in Kumasi after a police officer kicked her; Ghana criminalises same-sex conduct via a colonial-era law that is rarely enforced, but unlike some neighbours has not stiffened penalties - documents pervasive violence and discrimination.

Bachelor thesis (Diaconia University of Applied Sciences, Helsinki, 2017) by Seree Yeboa-Mensa: survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland on LGBT rights in Ghana - most opposed decriminalisation/legalisation, citing religio-cultural reasons and effects on children; most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.

GHA.tangentialFactors: “Unnatural carnal knowledge” (up to 3 years) criminalises same-sex conduct — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the lapsed bill would have criminalised identity itself.
GHA.comparisons: Pairwise: above Nigeria (0.19 — SSMPA in force with mob lynching culture) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts). Ghana's near-passage of an identity-criminalising bill is what separates it from Elevated band: the legal floor is currently the old 3-year statute, but the demonstrated legislative intent is far harsher.

This is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed an anti-LGBT "family values" bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for "promotion." The president refused to assent pending legal challenges, the supreme court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when parliament dissolved at the end of its term — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, "unnatural carnal knowledge" carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The capital has a resilient underground community (one LGBT+ organisation's 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.
GHA.blindOutOfScope: The 2024 bill never became law (lapsed unassented); its significance is climate/trajectory.

MAR.name: Morocco
MAR.summary:
Morocco is High Risk for trans visitors. Article 489 criminalises same-sex “indecent acts” (6 months–3 years), and Cairo 52 documents that trans people face de-facto criminalisation under Article 498 morality provisions — arrests based on gender-expression discrepancies and forced outing. The 2026 Cairo 52 report “A Web of Violence” describes a legal-medical-social system of erasure for trans people, including a de facto prohibition on transition care.

Visitor-relevant cases exist: in 2024, Brazilian influencer Liziane Gutierrez was arrested in Marrakesh, accused by police of being transgender, and alleges she was forced to show her genitals — she spent a month in jail. In 2019, Marrakesh police filmed and humiliated a cross-dressing man after a traffic accident, leaking the video online. There is no LGR framework and police have wide discretion; tourist areas (Marrakesh, Agadir) are more tolerant in practice but the legal exposure is constant.

The Gutierrez case demonstrates that even a cisgender visitor suspected of being trans can face genital inspection and jail.
MAR.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; the 2024 Gutierrez arrest was officially for filming a policeman — the trans-suspicion genital inspection is her allegation, disputed by Morocco.

Cairo 52 country review of Morocco: no specific provisions on transition, but de facto criminalisation under Article 498 (moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies, involuntary outing); no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only; the Grand Mufti opposes transition.
Hindustan Times (Nov 2024): an Instagram model alleges Moroccan police forced her to show her genitals over trans suspicions - reported police abuse of a trans woman based on appearance.

El País (Jan 2019): Moroccan police subjected a Marrakesh cross-dresser to online humiliation - after a minor traffic accident, Chafiq was handcuffed and filmed by bystanders and police officers, who also photographed his ID documents and posted them online; he sought asylum in Europe. Homosexuality is punishable in Morocco.

DZA.name: Algeria
DZA.summary:
Algeria is High Risk for trans visitors. Gender transition is not explicitly criminalised, but Cairo 52 documents that it is effectively criminalised through Penal Code Articles 333, 338, and 333 bis (indecency provisions), and NGOs have documented arrests of LGBT+ people under these articles. Same-sex activity itself carries up to 2 years under Article 338. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and no visible community infrastructure — activism operates almost entirely underground.

Unlike Tunisia or Morocco, Algeria lacks even a documented trans-visitor incident — partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access. The legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor (indecency arrest) is real but the enforcement pattern is thinner than Egypt's entrapment machinery or Tunisia's 2024-25 arrest wave.
DZA.outOfScopeNotes: Indecency-law application to trans people is documented in aggregate, not per-case; tourism volume is very low.

TUN.name: Tunisia
TUN.summary:
Tunisia is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — the country is in an active crackdown. Between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025, authorities arrested at least 84 people in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity — mostly gay men and transgender women, per Amnesty International. Penal Code Articles 226 bis (public indecency) and 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women.

In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where local NGO Intersection documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as “mental illness.” Since President Saied's 2021 power consolidation, the post-revolution space for LGBT organising (Shams, Damj) has been crushed — Shams was dissolved.
TUN.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is statutory context; the 2024-25 wave explicitly targeted trans women on gender-identity grounds.

sources.summary: Amnesty International (Feb 2025): Tunisia steps up crackdown on LGBTI individuals with a wave of arrests - at least 84 people (mainly gay men and trans women) arrested, arbitrarily detained and unjustly prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, solely based on actual or perceived SOGI, per Damj Association.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying Middle East Eye piece covered the same Tunisian crackdown arrests.

Cairo 52 country review of Tunisia: gender identities/expressions deviating from norms are effectively criminalised via Penal Code Articles 226 bis and 230, disproportionately targeting trans women; no comprehensive legal gender recognition framework - inconsistent rulings relying on judges' personal views and Sharia interpretations; gender-affirming care accessible only through well-informed medical professionals.

Intersection Association (Nov 2024): transgender women in Tunisian prisons endure continuous suffering - processed under former names and gender identification in all official procedures; forced shaving on entry without consent causes profound psychological harm, targeting the essence of their gender identity.

Cairo 52 (Jan 2024): the Tunis Court of First Instance (April 2023) declined legal gender recognition to a trans man, asserting insufficient evidence of a biological medical condition and dismissing gender identity disorder as a mental illness not fulfilling LGR criteria - reasoning based on comparative law from Egypt, ECtHR case-law and Dar Al-Ifta religious opinions.
HRW (March 2016): 'Tunisia: Men Prosecuted for Homosexuality' - documents prosecutions under Article 230 and the use of forced anal examinations as 'evidence'.

GayLawNet laws page for Tunisia: the 2012 draft bill punishing 'insulting the sanctity of religion'; courts refused to ban the LGBT radio station Shams Rad (2018) and upheld Shams's right to exist (2019) against government shutdown efforts.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Sept 2017): Tunisia pledged to the UN to stop forced anal testing (minister Mehdi Ben Gharbia in Geneva) but did not accept repeal of Article 230 (up to 3 years); Shams president Mounir Baatour was unenthusiastic - the abusive 'test' was dropped but the law remains.

TUN.tangentialFactors: Article 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the 2024-25 arrest wave explicitly included trans women on gender-identity grounds.
TUN.comparisons: Pairwise: below Egypt (0.22) and Algeria (0.22) on the strength of the current documented arrest wave explicitly including trans women; above Uganda (0.17 — death-penalty statute and lynching culture Tunisia lacks). Tunisia's trajectory is among the world's worst right now.

CMR.name: Cameroon
CMR.summary:
Cameroon is High Risk for trans visitors. The Shakiro case is the defining documentation: in February 2021, trans women Shakiro and Patricia were arrested in a Douala restaurant for the clothes they were wearing, convicted of “attempted homosexuality,” “indecent dressing” and ID irregularities, and sentenced to five years. They described five months of “hell” in Douala's central prison, initially in leg chains, before release pending appeal; Shakiro later received asylum in Belgium. Article 347-1 criminalises same-sex acts (up to 5 years), and Cameroon has among Africa's highest prosecution rates.

Police and mob violence against perceived LGBT people are both documented, and there is no legal gender recognition or protection of any kind. The Shakiro conviction shows that visible trans expression in a public place is itself treated as a prosecutable offence.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation in public risks arrest on indecency/ID grounds; prison conditions are severe.
CMR.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; the Shakiro case demonstrates direct application to gender expression.

TZA.name: Tanzania
TZA.summary:
Tanzania is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex activity with up to life imprisonment, and the political environment has been actively hostile since the Magufuli-era crackdowns (arrests, forced anal examinations documented by HRW in earlier years, de-registration of LGBT-serving organisations). The 2024 case of Mauzinde is emblematic: a transgender woman and activist found abandoned in a forest in Rahaleo, beaten, her ears cut off — an attack the UN Human Rights Office called “horrendous.”

OONI documented extensive targeted blocking of LGBTQ websites correlating with the escalating crackdown, and Amnesty's 2024 regional report notes Tanzanian pushes to further criminalise LGBT people. Zanzibar has its own, harsher penal code. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest under indecency provisions and mob violence; Zanzibar is worse than the mainland.
TZA.outOfScopeNotes: Life-imprisonment statute is same-sex (climate/situational); the Mauzinde attack is trans-specific.

ETH.name: Ethiopia
ETH.summary:
Ethiopia is High Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is criminalised (up to 1 year, or more under aggravating provisions), and because Ethiopia has no legal gender recognition, trans people are legally treated as their birth sex — meaning a trans person's ordinary relationships can be prosecuted as same-sex conduct. The 2024 UPR stakeholder report documents discrimination, violence, and absence of police protection, with trans women and queer women particularly at risk, plus a growing organised anti-LGBTQ+ campaign inside the country.

Documented trans-specific enforcement is thinner than Cameroon's or Tunisia's — Ethiopia's LGBTQ+ community (self-identified as “zega”) is deeply underground, and reporting is sparse — but the legal structure (criminalisation + no LGR catch-all), hostile campaigning, and absence of any protection place it firmly in High Risk. Digital surveillance and blackmail vulnerability are noted in the UPR reporting.
ETH.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation captures trans people via birth-sex legal status — a direct, not situational, mechanism.

LBN.name: Lebanon
LBN.summary:
Lebanon is High Risk for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced, and Cairo 52 documents rising prejudice and violence against trans people, particularly trans women, who face entrenched marginalisation and family/community violence.

For a visitor: Beirut is navigable with discretion; visible trans feminine expression carries real (statutory) arrest risk; the economic collapse has degraded police predictability in both directions.
LBN.outOfScopeNotes: LGR case law and healthcare pathologisation are resident-facing; Art 521/534 are the traveler-relevant statutes.

JOR.name: Jordan
JOR.summary:
Jordan is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — the safest of the Levantine Arab states by a clear margin, but on a deteriorating trajectory. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 1951, and courts have granted legal gender recognition in individual cases (the 2014 Court of Cassation ruling — though justified by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex). There is no statute criminalising gender expression itself.

The deterioration is documented: Cairo 52 reports a notable rise in targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, using Ottoman/British-era morality laws; Jordanian security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activities; the 2023 cybercrime law (“inciting immorality”) gives authorities a digital tool against LGBT expression; and gender-affirming surgery is criminalised for trans people (Article 8, Medical and Health Liability Law) while permitted for intersex people. In 2021 security forces arrested 14 people at a private party.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression per se, but morality-law discretion, shuttered community infrastructure, and family-society hostility make outing dangerous.
JOR.outOfScopeNotes: Surgery criminalisation and LGR case law are resident-facing; morality-law and cybercrime enforcement are the traveler-relevant mechanisms.

IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.summary:
Iraq is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — it now has one of the world's most explicitly anti-trans statutes, in force since 1 July 2024. Amendments to the 1988 anti-prostitution law criminalise same-sex relationships (10–15 years), “biological sex change based on personal desire and inclination” (criminalising transition itself), and men who “intentionally act like women” (1–3 years) — a direct statutory criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Promoting homosexuality carries a minimum 7-year sentence. President Rashid signed the law on 29 June 2024.

Behind the statute stands a documented milieu of lethal violence: militia-led campaigns against men perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming (HRW's “They Want Us Exterminated” documented mutilated bodies dumped as warnings), with impunity. Most LGBT Iraqis hide their identity entirely. The Kurdistan Region has not passed the federal law but shares the social climate and has no protections.

For a visitor: being visibly trans is a statutory offence; discovery risks 1–3 years, with severe custodial and militia risk beyond the legal penalty.
IRQ.outOfScopeNotes: The 1988-law amendments apply in federal Iraq; the suspended KRI parliament has not adopted them, but no protection exists there either.

VEN.name: Venezuela
VEN.summary:
Venezuela is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing about gender expression is criminalised, but Venezuela has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid the broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents.

Caracas has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.
VEN.outOfScopeNotes: General humanitarian and repression context affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific protection vacuum.

BOL.name: Bolivia
BOL.summary:
Bolivia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — one of Latin America's legal pioneers on paper. The 2016 Gender Identity Law was ground-breaking: legal gender recognition on the basis of self-declared identity (administrative process, no surgery), and gender identity is an explicitly protected ground in anti-discrimination law. Bolivia's constitution also names gender identity.

Implementation lags the statute: the first national LGBTQ+ survey (2024) reveals significant exclusion in health, education, employment, and housing; social conservatism is strong outside La Paz/Santa Cruz; and bureaucrats often resist applying the Gender Identity Law. There is no documented pattern of police targeting of trans people as such, and no traveler-facing restriction — but also limited effective protection outside major cities.
BOL.outOfScopeNotes: LGR mechanics and discrimination-law enforcement gaps are resident-facing.

PRY.name: Paraguay
PRY.summary:
Paraguay is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — South America's most conservative country. There is no legal gender recognition (ten lawsuits on trans name recognition remain pending, unresolved), no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. AP documents that many LGBTQ+ Paraguayans feel compelled to leave their hometowns due to discrimination, harassment, and gender-based violence; trans women face particular social rejection. Amnesty reports persistent structural discrimination and high gender-based violence.

Nothing criminalises being trans, Asunción has a small organised community, and there is no documented police targeting pattern — the risk is social hostility and a total protection vacuum rather than state persecution. Tourist traffic is low and there are no documented trans-visitor incidents.
PRY.outOfScopeNotes: Pending LGR lawsuits and discrimination-law absence are resident-facing.

GTM.name: Guatemala
GTM.summary:
Guatemala is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022, with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” law, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (Lambda, trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.
GTM.outOfScopeNotes: General gang violence affects all travelers; femicide-law exclusion is resident-facing but signals institutional stance.

HND.name: Honduras
HND.summary:
Honduras is High Risk for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the hemisphere outside Brazil/Mexico.
HND.outOfScopeNotes: Gang violence affects everyone; the score reflects the trans-specific documented pattern and state-responsibility finding.

SLV.name: El Salvador
SLV.summary:
El Salvador is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception with mass arbitrary detention (75,000+ imprisoned, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.
SLV.outOfScopeNotes: The state of exception affects all travelers; its trans-specific application is a risk mechanism, not a documented pattern.

CRI.name: Costa Rica
CRI.summary:
Costa Rica is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.
CRI.outOfScopeNotes: ID sex-marker limits and Church influence are resident-facing/climate.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal since 1971; first Central American country with marriage equality (2020); since 2018 trans people can change legal gender without surgery or judicial intervention (Executive Decree N° 41173-MP instructs public institutions to update records per self-perceived gender identity); the state health system funds gender-affirming care; the progressive agenda faces increasing conservative resistance and paralysis.
NOTE: Page content did not load at fetch time (the ILGA World database returned only a 'Loading' placeholder - JavaScript-only page).

UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, report on her July 2023 visit to Costa Rica (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024): praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific legislation; concerned about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups; recommends intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

IGLHRC/CWGL report 'Written Out: How Sexuality Is Used to Attack Women's Organizing' (revised 2005): documents how sexuality is weaponised against women's organising internationally, including 'basics of baiting: internationalizing intolerance' - context for Costa Rica among case countries.

GayLawNet Costa Rica laws page: age of consent 18 for same-sex couples (2008); survivor's pensions extended to same-sex couples (2016-2018, Ministry of Labor and Social Security); documents the incremental legal recognition timeline.

DOM.name: Dominican Republic
DOM.summary:

Same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, but strikingly, Articles 210/260 still criminalise it for police and armed-forces members — challenged at the Constitutional Court in August 2024, revealing the institutional culture. CAN.name: Canada
CAN.summary:
Canada is Low Risk for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveler warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets.
CAN.outOfScopeNotes: Provincial healthcare/school policy rollbacks are resident-facing climate signals.

AUS.name: Australia
AUS.summary:
Australia is Low Risk for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court's landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability.

NZL.name: New Zealand
NZL.summary:
New Zealand is Low Risk for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration has been in force since 2023 (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act); the Law Commission reviewed Human Rights Act protections for trans, non-binary and intersex people in 2024; and takatāpui/rainbow communities have deep institutional recognition. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

The counterweights are documented and significant: reports of gender-identity hate crimes jumped 42% between 2022 and 2023 (161 to 229 incidents), spiking around the Posie Parker visit; the Counting Ourselves survey found almost 1 in 5 trans and non-binary people were threatened with physical violence in four years, and 8% experienced it; and community advocates accuse police of failing rainbow communities amid far-right agitation (library events crashed, church arson threats). New Zealand's global-progressive reputation outruns its current street climate.

For a visitor: full legal protection; moderate probability of harassment in charged spaces; functioning (if criticised) institutions.
NZL.outOfScopeNotes: Counting Ourselves data is resident-survey-based; healthcare gaps are resident-facing.

ALB.name: Albania
ALB.summary:
Albania is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; a National LGBTI Action Plan (2021–2027) is in force (implementation is admittedly flawed); and the UN Independent Expert on SOGI conducted a full country visit in July 2024 — a sign of government openness unusual for the region. Tirana hosts an annual Pride.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, no bathroom laws, no documented police targeting; the realistic risk is social hostility outside Tirana and along more conservative rural areas. EU candidate status is driving slow alignment.

MKD.name: North Macedonia
MKD.summary:
North Macedonia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised, and Skopje hosts both Pride and an organised Trans March for Visibility (TransFormA, March 2024) — public trans organising that proceeds without serious incident. Anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and gender identity (2019 amendments). Counterweights: hate speech and hate crimes remain common with no effective justice-system response (European Commission), social-media death threats are routine, and there is no legal gender recognition.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; small but functioning community; standard Balkan street-hostility caution.

MNE.name: Montenegro
MNE.summary:
Montenegro is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — the Western Balkans' most advanced legal framework. It has a same-sex partnership law (2020), anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and SOGI-inclusive hate-crime provisions; Podgorica Pride proceeds annually. Counterweights documented by ILGA-Europe: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric is a serious issue, and misdemeanour charges are overused in place of proper hate-crime prosecution (European Commission). There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative practice is inconsistent).

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, small tolerant coastal tourist scene; standard caution in the north.
MNE.outOfScopeNotes: LGR inconsistency and prosecution-practice gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Montenegro: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric continued; a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on TV was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks (police response monitored); a groundbreaking study found only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation; a new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with €45,000; over 222 online hate-speech incidents reported.
Human Dignity Trust: 'A History of LGBT Criminalisation' - overview of criminalising jurisdictions and strategic litigation (Montenegro context: decriminalised in 1977 under Yugoslavia).

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montenegro: Past and Present' (March 2012): decriminalised in 1977; both male and female same-sex activity legal; equal age of consent at 14; same-sex couples lack the legal rights of married couples - historical and cultural context from Ottoman rule to independence.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2013): Montenegro's first Podgorica Pride - ~2,000 police guarded ~150 marchers; tear gas used against rock-throwing opponents; organiser Danijel Kalezic: 'From this day we are no longer invisible'; the march seen as a test of Montenegro's EU human-rights commitments.

PinkNews (Aug 2019): Montenegro's politicians blocked the same-sex partnership law (July 31) despite backing from the governing DPS; conservative Democratic Front deputy Jovan Vucurovic: 'After this law a law on adoption of children by LGBT population will follow'; the Equal Rights Association said LGBT+ people are 'forced to live in hiding'.

CDM/Dan (Dec 2018): the Government defined the Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership - granting same-sex couples the same rights as heterosexuals except parenting: no fostering, no adoption; law to enter into force one year after parliamentary adoption.

MNE.localsOnly: No LGR law (administrative practice inconsistent) — resident-facing; the misdemeanour-overuse practice affects resident victims.
MNE.comparisons: After the 2026-08 audit: the audit found Montenegro’s framework (partnership law + SOGI hate-crime provisions + protected Pride) objectively stronger than Hungary’s (propaganda law in force + LGR ban + German court’s extradition-refusal finding). BIH.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
BIH.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; Sarajevo Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 with heavy (necessary) police protection; and most cantons have now appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes — genuine institutional progress. Counterweights from the 2024 Pink Report: negative events are accumulating, the trend is unfavourable outside Sarajevo (especially Republika Srpska), and trans people occupy a “precarious position” — no legal gender recognition framework, restricted healthcare access, and institutional suspicion. The state is also deeply dysfunctional generally.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; stick to Sarajevo and tourist areas; avoid visible trans presentation in Republika Srpska and rural areas.
BIH.outOfScopeNotes: Entity-level (Republika Srpska) hostility varies; LGR absence is resident-facing.

sources.summary: Sarajevo Open Centre's Pink Report 2024 (annual report on the human rights of LGBT persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina): the position of LGBTI people is unsatisfactory nationwide with a growing disparity between the two entities. In Republika Srpska there was an organised hooligan attack on BH Pride March activists in Banja Luka, incitement to violence and discrimination by the entity's highest officials, and organised anti-LGBT groups.

Balkan Diskurs feature (Oct 2024): legal gender recognition is formally accessible across BiH but described as vague and ineffective in practice - legal texts imply it requires complete medical transition, contradicting self-determination (criticised by the European Parliament). Without documents matching appearance, trans people face difficulties accessing housing and jobs; medical transition becomes a prerequisite for basic rights.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on BiH: eight SOGIESC hate-speech cases documented ahead of Sarajevo Pride; prosecutor offices in the majority of cantons now have staff overseeing anti-LGBTI hate crimes; the Federal Government instructed the Justice Ministry to draft a same-sex partnership law; the first Constitutional Court appeal was filed over non-recognition of a Croatian-issued same-sex partnership; extremists roamed Banja Luka chanting 'kill the...' before Pride events.

Sarajevo Open Centre (July 2016): the Federation of BiH adopted hate-crime regulation covering sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances - all three BiH administrative units now regulate hate crimes in their criminal codes.

GEO.name: Georgia
GEO.summary:
Georgia is High Risk for trans visitors — and deteriorating fast. In September 2024 parliament passed the Russia-style law “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”: it bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, LGBT public assembly, and dissemination of LGBT information — the region's harshest legislative package outside Russia itself. One day after passage, Kesaria Abramidze, one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her Tbilisi apartment; mourners and AP drew a direct line between the law's rhetoric and the killing.

This compounds an existing pattern: the 2021 Pride office ransacking by far-right mobs while police stood by, the foreign-agents law choking LGBT NGOs (which refuse to register and face bankruptcy), and documented police failure to protect demonstrators (Identoba v. Georgia ECtHR line of cases, still unimplemented). Georgia's visible trans community is now legally erased and physically targeted.

For a visitor: being visibly trans in Georgia now carries both statutory risk (assembly/information provisions) and elevated street-violence risk, with police as unreliable protectors.
GEO.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 law’s healthcare and LGR provisions are resident-facing; its assembly/information provisions can reach visitors.

Rights groups linked the killing to the government's promotion of the law; the President called it 'horrendous'. The law bans same-sex marriage, gender-affirming surgeries, adoption by non-heterosexuals, and 'promotion' of same-sex relationships in schools.
NOTE: Page content did not load at fetch time (only AP site navigation was retrieved); the underlying article covers Georgia's crackdown on LGBTQ rights in the election context.

Georgia): ineffective investigations into police misconduct and failure to protect demonstrators from homophobic/transphobic violence; risk of statutes of limitations expiring; new regressive anti-LGBTI legislative initiatives.

ARM.name: Armenia
ARM.summary:
Armenia is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Armenia has no anti-LGBT legislation of the Georgian or Russian type — and an administrative practice for legal gender recognition exists (medicalised). Pink Armenia's 2024 annual report documents ongoing violations including inhuman/degrading treatment, and hate speech is routine in public discourse; the 2018 failed anti-discrimination bill means there is still no SOGI-specific protection statute. Yerevan has a small organised community (Pink Armenia, Right Side — a trans-led NGO), but visibility carries real risk.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; social hostility significant outside central Yerevan; police response unreliable.
ARM.outOfScopeNotes: Protection-statute absence and LGR medicalisation are resident-facing.

sources.summary: Pink Human Rights Defender NGO annual report on the human rights situation of LGBT+ people in Armenia during 2024. Documents discrimination, torture and inhuman/degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and hate speech - including a chapter on pressure around a transgender individual participating in a beauty pageant.

Equaldex comparison of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia: Armenia decriminalised in 2003; legal gender change is legal but requires surgery (since 2006); gender-affirming care is restricted; no nonbinary recognition; hate-crime protections 'ambiguous' since 2022; no SOGI discrimination protections; same-sex marriage banned. Public-opinion acceptance scores are very low (5/100).

ILGA-Europe/COC fact-finding report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, HIV/AIDS, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in Armenia.

Unzipped: Gay Armenia blog (May 2012): neo-Nazi arson attack on the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan - Molotov cocktail thrown, fire set; police took 12 hours to respond; two suspects detained via CCTV - documents anti-LGBT hate violence in Armenia.

The Guardian (April 2019): Armenia's first registered trans woman, Lilit Martirosyan, received death threats (including MPs calling for her to be burned alive) after a historic speech in the national assembly on LGBTI discrimination - documents extreme political hostility toward trans people.

AZE.name: Azerbaijan
AZE.summary:
Azerbaijan is High Risk for trans visitors. The documented pattern is grim: a trans woman was tortured and murdered in Baku in July 2023; a second trans woman's murder in March 2024 was met with a police response lacking comprehensive investigation; several other trans people were physically assaulted, including by police themselves; and two trans women were detained for “hooliganism” for making noise. Government-affiliated media air targeted discriminatory hate speech. Trans people face total economic marginalisation (black-market work, precarious housing).

Nothing formally criminalises gender expression, but police are perpetrators rather than protectors, and the state is one of the world's more closed authoritarian systems — there is no recourse and no community infrastructure that can operate openly. An April 2024 ECtHR ruling found violations in Azerbaijan's treatment of LGBTI applicants.

For a visitor: no statute bars entry or expression, but discovery risks police abuse with no remedy, and the murder-impunity pattern is documented.
AZE.outOfScopeNotes: Economic exclusion data is resident-facing; police-perpetrator pattern is traveler-relevant.

KAZ.name: Kazakhstan
KAZ.summary:
Kazakhstan is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — Central Asia's most liveable country for trans people, which is a relative statement. Nothing is criminalised; legal gender recognition exists (heavily medicalised: psychiatric boards, and surgery requirements applied in practice); and revealingly, hundreds of trans people fled TO Kazakhstan from Russia after its propaganda law and LGR ban. ODIHR recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in 2024 — real, but documented and reported, which itself indicates functioning civil society (Feminita, ECOM).

The trajectory is the concern: a “We Are Against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda” petition gained official review by the Ministry of Culture in 2024 (HRW urged rejection), and anti-gender MPs are vocal. Currently there is no propaganda statute, no bathroom law, and no police targeting pattern — police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; low visibility = low risk; Almaty/Astana are navigable.
KAZ.outOfScopeNotes: LGR medicalisation and the propaganda petition are resident-facing/trajectory signals.

UZB.name: Uzbekistan
UZB.summary:
Uzbekistan is High Risk for trans visitors. Article 120 of the Criminal Code criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 3 years) — and Human Dignity Trust notes transgender people may be targeted under it, since there is no legal gender recognition and trans people are legally their birth sex. There is substantial evidence of recent enforcement: frequent arrests, and extortion by threat of arrest, with police as the most common perpetrators of anti-LGBT violence; torture goes unpunished (HRW). Because of criminalisation, victims cannot report violence to authorities.

ECOM's 2024 national report documents continuing rights violations, and the Justice Ministry denies registration to independent human-rights groups — no community infrastructure can operate openly. There is no documented trans-visitor case, but the legal mechanism (birth-sex status + Art 120) means a trans visitor discovered in a same-sex-appearing relationship faces direct prosecution risk, and discovery itself invites extortion.
UZB.outOfScopeNotes: Art 120 formally applies to male same-sex conduct; its application to trans people is via birth-sex legal status — a direct mechanism, not merely climate.

NIC.name: Nicaragua
NIC.summary: Nicaragua is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans (sodomy was decriminalised in 2008), but NGOs document 108 cases of violence against the LGTBIQ+ community in 2024 alone, and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years. Since 2018 the Ortega regime has shut down or exiled virtually all independent civil society — including LGBT organisations — so there is no domestic protection infrastructure and no recourse; arbitrary detention is used broadly against perceived opponents.
NIC.outOfScopeNotes: Generalised repression affects all; the trans-murder count is trans-specific.

GUY.name: Guyana
GUY.summary:
Guyana is High Risk for trans visitors — one of only five Western-Hemisphere countries still criminalising same-sex conduct (buggery carries life imprisonment on paper, though rarely enforced). The IACHR heard evidence in November 2024 of severe violence against trans women: 69 cases of violence against trans women documented 2018–2022, in a country of under a million people. Police fail to investigate anti-LGBT violence; there is no anti-discrimination legislation (the UN Human Rights Committee called for it in April 2024) and no legal gender recognition.

Cross-dressing was decriminalised after a 2018 CCJ ruling (McEwan v AG), removing the most direct trans-expression statute, but the climate and investigative failure keep risk high. Georgetown has a small organised community (SASOD).
GUY.outOfScopeNotes: Buggery statutes are rarely enforced (climate/situational); the CCJ struck cross-dressing laws in 2018.

SUR.name: Suriname
SUR.summary:
Suriname is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — legally unremarkable, socially mixed. Same-sex conduct is legal; the constitution's “any other status” clause is read to cover SOGI discrimination; and the 2022 Equal Treatment Labour Act added employment protections. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-murder pattern, but Paramaribo's small community reports routine harassment, and the interior has essentially no protection.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest street risk in Paramaribo; low tourist infrastructure generally.
SUR.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and interior governance gaps are resident-facing.

Paris Yvanna Simson ordering registration changes for a trans woman.

Civil society report (Projekta Foundation with VIDS and LGBT Platform Suriname) to the UN Human Rights Committee's 141st session (July 2024) on ICCPR implementation in Suriname - includes non-discrimination and gender-equality sections covering LGBT issues.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Suriname: documents the Bouterse trial, police brutality, corruption, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities'.

LGBT Platform Suriname + Akahatá + Heartland Alliance stakeholder report (Oct 2015) to the Human Rights Committee: the March 2015 Penal Code revisions (Articles 175, 175a, 176) added sexual-orientation protections (1 year jail or fine for discrimination), but implementation lags; government members' anti-gay positions and media/music-industry hostility perpetuate homophobia.

UN Geneva meeting summary (July 2024): Human Rights Committee experts commended Suriname's commitment to judicial independence during its fourth ICCPR periodic-report review, asking about the National Human Rights Institute and indigenous rights.

Suriname LGBT Platform UPR pre-session summary (March 2016): since the 2011 UPR, Suriname equalised the age of consent and added discrimination provisions (2015); but the pension act excludes same-sex couples from survivor pensions contrary to the constitution's non-discrimination principle; the Platform has never been included in consultative processes.

SUR.localsOnly: No LGR — resident-facing; the 2022 labour act and the harassment reports concern residents.
SUR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Ecuador (0.57 — far less violence) and below India (0.58, tie).

KGZ.name: Kyrgyzstan
KGZ.summary:
Kyrgyzstan is High Risk for trans visitors — once Central Asia's relative haven, now regressing. In 2023-2024 Kyrgyzstan adopted two discriminatory laws targeting the LGBTI community and restricting LGBTI organisations, accompanied by homophobic/transphobic MP rhetoric; TGEU records Kyrgyzstan (2021) among the countries that removed legal gender recognition entirely (the 2020 Civil Status Acts law blocks birth-certificate changes). Same-sex conduct is legal (1998), but police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and the community (Kyrgyz Indigo) operates under pressure.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but LGR removal + police extortion culture + active anti-LGBT political campaign make outing risky.
KGZ.outOfScopeNotes: LGR removal is resident-facing; NGO-restriction laws signal the enforcement climate.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Kyrgyzstan: two discriminatory laws (2023-2024) target the LGBTI community and restrict organisations, amid homophobic political rhetoric; since 2021 trans people cannot obtain legal recognition (Law on Civil Acts amendments); in 2024 Article 47 of the Health Law was amended to bar gender-transition-related medical examination or treatment until age 25 (previously 18); ECOM data show high stigma from law enforcement and healthcare workers, with police abuse of power.

TGEU Trans Rights Index & Map 2024 launch (May 2024): documents polarisation in trans rights across Europe and Central Asia - progress in some countries (Greece, Iceland topping the ranking) and alarming regressions elsewhere, notably Russia's July 2023 ban on medical and legal transition; two new indicators added for 2024.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity decriminalised 1998 (equal age of consent 16); 2016 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage; the provision allowing some trans people to change markers was removed in 2020; in early 2026 an MP proposed a bill defining sex as immutable, explicitly banning legal gender recognition and prohibiting any interventions on minors; follows the 2023-2024 'silencing' laws.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and HRT across the EECA region (with country coordinators for Georgia, Armenia, Ukraine, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Moldova, Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan, Tajikistan) - includes information for trans migrants.

HRW World Report 2020, Kyrgyzstan chapter: includes a Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section - documents the worsening environment for LGBT people, including the 'gay propaganda' bill and violence against women.

RFE/RL (June 2017): 'Curtain Falls On Bishkek's Lone LGBT Club Amid Worsening Atmosphere' - the London club in Bishkek closed; founder Olesya: 'people don't understand what a gay club is... they think we are doing something pornographic. But if they came and saw that it is just a normal club... it would be OK.'

The Guardian (Oct 2017): 'All of us will be victims at some point': why Bishkek's only gay club closed - the Kyrgyz capital was long a liberal beacon in Central Asia until the 'LGBT propaganda' ban; with attacks and rapes on the rise, the community is scared.

KGZ.localsOnly: The 2020 law blocking birth-certificate changes (LGR removal) is resident-facing; the NGO-restriction laws affect resident organisations.
KGZ.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Lebanon (0.36 — different mechanisms: KGZ has NGO-restriction laws and LGR removal; LBN has Art 521/534), below Georgia (0.38 — Georgia's 2024 package is broader) and above Sri Lanka (0.33).

In 2023-2024 it adopted two discriminatory laws targeting the LGBTI community and restricting LGBTI organisations, accompanied by homophobic and transphobic rhetoric from legislators; a trans-rights monitoring network lists it (2021) among the countries that removed legal gender recognition entirely (a 2020 civil-registry law blocks birth-certificate changes). Same-sex conduct is legal (1998), but police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and the community's main organisation operates under pressure.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but the legal-gender-recognition removal plus a police extortion culture and an active anti-LGBT political campaign make outing risky.

TJK.name: Tajikistan
TJK.summary:
Tajikistan is High Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation (IPHR 2024) shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition (a medicalised registration route exists on paper under the Civil Status Acts law), no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids + registry practices + zero recourse make discovery dangerous.
TJK.outOfScopeNotes: Registry practices and raid patterns target residents but define the enforcement climate for any discovered trans person.

sources.summary: IPHR report 'Rights for All? LGBTIQ Persons in Tajikistan Systematically Denied Human Rights' (Feb 2024): documents widespread homophobia/transphobia, human-rights violations, the 2016 police register of LGBTIQ people, 2022/2023 police raids with forced HIV-testing and arbitrary criminal charges, ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police, privacy violations followed by 'pornography' prosecutions, and additional problems facing trans people.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex acts not criminalised since independence; no SOGISC non-discrimination protections; no transparent legal gender recognition procedure, though at least two trans men and one trans woman changed markers via court in 2023; nonconsensual intersex interventions legal; in 2024 ECOM recorded 27 cases of human-rights violations against LGBT people, with police arbitrary arrests, blackmail and extortion.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention/treatment and HRT across the EECA region (with country coordinators including Tajikistan), including information for trans migrants.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025, Tajikistan chapter (covering 2024): Russia's anti-LGBTI laws have influenced Tajikistan; coming out risks family shame leading to sham marriages - one person was beaten, tied up without food and forcibly married, with police taking no action; in Sughd, 10+ cases of police luring LGBT people into fake meetings to register them in a database and extort money; the 2022 anti-discrimination law dropped SOGI, leaving only 'sex'.

ECOM legislative analysis (2020): 'Legislative analysis related to SOGI and HIV in Tajikistan' - identifies legal barriers for gay men, other MSM and trans people, analysing legislation and law-enforcement practice against international standards, with local partners.

HRW World Report 2017, Tajikistan chapter: the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016 - opposition leaders sentenced, lawyers imprisoned, a predetermined referendum allowing President Rahmon to rule for life - the repressive context for LGBT life.

Global Voices (Jan 2013) by Alexander Sodiqov: 'Tajikistan Remains Hell for Gays' - despite decriminalisation 15 years earlier, there is very little tolerance; those who come out become targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police; the LGBT community remains 'one of the most closed and secretive parts of Tajik society'; sparked by a violent university incident.

TJK.localsOnly: The informal LGBT registries and the on-paper medicalised LGR route are resident-facing; the raid pattern primarily targets residents but defines the enforcement climate for any discovered trans person.
TJK.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Malaysia (0.28 — different mechanisms: TJK has police raids without statutes; MYS has Sharia statutes), below Azerbaijan (0.30) and above Pakistan (0.26).

TKM.name: Turkmenistan
TKM.summary:
Turkmenistan is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 2 years under Article 135) and, more fundamentally, Turkmenistan is one of the world's most closed states: the state exerts strict media control and heavy internet monitoring, no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible since 2019, and asylum is the community's most urgent need (ILGA-Europe). Amnesty has documented systematic abuses. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, no recourse, and no visibility — the only safe strategy is total concealment.

For a visitor: any discoverable online presence or visible nonconformity is dangerous in a state that monitors communications pervasively.
TKM.outOfScopeNotes: Absence of documentation is itself evidence of severity: data collection is impossible because it is unsafe.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Turkmenistan: asylum remains one of the most urgent needs for the LGBTI community; the only documented research on LGBTI issues dates to 2019 (data collection almost impossible due to safety risks); Amnesty documented systemic discrimination; the April 2022 Criminal Code kept 'sodomy' provisions and increased the severity and scope of punishments; torture and inhumane treatment by law enforcement reported, with several LGBTI people forced to flee; the Ministry of National Security collaborates with regional AIDS centres, exposing HIV-test data.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Turkmenistan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under Article 135 (up to 2 years); societal stigma; the totalitarian state's pervasive repression.

EHPV (Estonian Network of People Living with HIV) mid-term UPR submission (2020) on Turkmenistan: LGBT persons and PLHIV 'have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights'; Article 135 criminalises consensual same-sex acts; LGBT persons are increasingly fleeing to the EU to seek refuge.

ECOM Legal Environment Assessment (2019, with Turkmen.news): legislative analysis related to LGBT rights and HIV in Turkmenistan - identifies legal barriers for PLHIV, gay men, MSM and trans people, analysing law-enforcement practice and international recommendations.
Columbia Law School (May 2007): the Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic secured asylum for a Turkmen woman who feared persecution because she is a lesbian in the mostly Muslim country.

Goldberg Kohn (Sept 2019): attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared persecution including imprisonment and torture; homosexuality is punishable by up to 2 years; suspects face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals; women are vulnerable to sexual violence and 'honor killings'.

TKM.tangentialFactors: Article 135 criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 2 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
TKM.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Qatar (0.12 — different profiles: TKM's opacity prevents even documenting abuse; QAT's abuse is documented), below Uzbekistan (0.22 — UZB has enforcement data and some civil society) and Russia (0.12, tie).

SYR.name: Syria
SYR.summary:
Syria is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Articles 520/517 of the Penal Code criminalise “sexual acts against nature” and public indecency; there is no legal gender recognition. Since the fall of the Assad regime (December 2024), the situation has worsened: the Guardians of Equality Movement documented “waves of violence” against Syrian transgender women in the first two months of 2025, implicating both non-state armed groups and security forces in multiple cities, and February 2025 videos showed authorities arresting trans women. Digital targeting (entrapment via apps, extortion) is documented across the conflict period.

For a visitor: active conflict, trans-targeted violence waves, no recourse whatsoever.
SYR.outOfScopeNotes: General conflict risk affects all; the 2025 trans-women violence waves are trans-specific.

sources.summary: NOTE: The Guardians of the Gem report on LGBTQIA individuals in Syria after the fall of the Assad regime (April 2025) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).
NOTE: Page content did not load at fetch time (only EUAA site navigation was retrieved); the underlying EUAA Syria Country Focus section 282 covers treatment by state, non-state and societal actors.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Articles 520 and 517 criminalise 'sexual acts against nature' and public indecency; no legal gender recognition and no prohibition of nonconsensual intersex interventions; during the 2011-2024 conflict, violence on SOGI grounds escalated - Islamist groups executed and publicly tortured sexual and gender minorities (particularly queer men and trans women); government forces arrested people on morality charges, committed enforced disappearances and sexual violence in detention.
HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Syria's Article 520 criminalisation and the situation of LGBT Syrians amid the conflict.

Syria Direct (Oct 2020): 'At home and abroad, LGBT Syrians fight to have their voices heard' - Amira al-Tabbaa's activism since 2004 helping those kicked out of work or home; in 'gay-friendly' Damascus cafes friends spoke 'only in whispers'; 'We need to break the door of the closet that they put us into and get out: We deserve life.'

Newsweek (2015): two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever UN Security Council meeting on LGBT rights (closed session, co-sponsored by the US and Chile) about constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

PinkNews (June 2010): Syrian authorities raided private gay parties, arresting over 25 men - charged with 'homosexual acts', drugs, or 'obscene' parties; families refused to pay bail; police monitor cruising areas; Gay Middle East called for repeal of the 'antiquated' Article 520 of the 1949 Penal Code.

SYR.tangentialFactors: Articles 520/517 criminalise “sexual acts against nature” — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
SYR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Saudi Arabia (0.05 — SYR's chaos vs SAU's systematic state machinery) and below Iraq (0.08 — IRQ now has a codified anti-trans statute; SYR has codified indecency + active violence waves).
