LBY.name: Libya
LBY.summary:
Libya is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “illicit sexual intercourse” and “indecent acts” (up to 5 years), and Cairo 52 documents de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and transition through these provisions — compounded by recent religious rulings declaring the very term “gender” haram, making anyone using it in media or institutions susceptible to prosecution. Militias control territory and operate detention sites where torture is systematic; there is no functioning central judiciary, no LGR, and no protection of any kind.

For a visitor: detention by any of several militia authorities is the modal bad outcome, with no consular reach in much of the country.
LBY.outOfScopeNotes: Militia fragmentation means enforcement varies by territory; the trans-specific mechanism is documented de-facto criminalisation.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 country review of Libya: de facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and transition (social, medical, surgical) via 'indecent acts' and 'illicit intercourse' provisions; recent religious rulings designate the term 'gender' as haram, exposing users to punishment; no legal gender recognition framework or court attempts; armed militias retaliate against gender-diverse people amid the post-2011 conflict.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity criminalised (up to 5 years under 'illicit sexual intercourse' and 'indecent acts' provisions applying to men and women); no SOGISC protections; no legal gender recognition; enforcement and repression intensified after 2011 - armed groups and security agencies arrest people based on perceived orientation or gender identity, with discrimination, violence and arbitrary detention.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Libya's criminalisation of same-sex activity.

The Guardian (June 2016): Brian Whitaker's 'Everything you need to know about being gay in Muslim countries' - the official fiction is that gay people don't exist in the Middle East; family and societal attitudes are often a bigger problem than state persecution; Libya among the countries covered.
HRW (June 2015): 'Islamic State's War on Gays' - documents ISIS executions of men accused of homosexuality in territories it controlled, including in Libya.

D+C (June 2015): 'The situation for homosexuals in Libya is getting worse' - ISIS executed three young men in Derna (kneeling in plastic tubs, shot in the back of the head before a crowd); considered the first death sentence against homosexuals in modern Libya's history; no one in Derna dares speak of the killings.

HuffPost (Nov 2012): report that 12 men accused of being gay faced torture and death by a Libyan militia - NOTE: the original source was a Facebook page falsely claiming HRW affiliation, which later apologised for misrepresenting itself; treat with caution.

LBY.tangentialFactors: “Illicit sexual intercourse” and “indecent acts” provisions (up to 5 years) capture same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity alike.
LBY.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Oman (0.09 — OMN has an explicit enforced statute; LBY has de-facto criminalisation plus militia detention risk), below Iraq (0.08, comparable) and above Syria (0.06).

Militias control territory and operate detention sites where torture is systematic; there is no functioning central judiciary, no legal gender recognition, and no protection of any kind.

For a visitor: detention by any of several militia authorities is the modal bad outcome, with no consular reach in much of the country.

YEM.name: Yemen
YEM.summary:
Yemen is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The legal framework criminalises same-sex conduct (up to death under some interpretations of the Penal Code; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise), but Cairo 52 emphasises the operative mechanism: the erosion of the rule of law and the power of militias has facilitated a surge in attacks targeting transgender individuals — de facto criminalisation operating outside any judicial system. Houthi-controlled areas impose their own moral-policing regime; the south has its own militia authorities.

For a visitor: no safe authority to appeal to anywhere in the country.
YEM.outOfScopeNotes: War risk affects all; the documented surge in trans-targeted attacks is trans-specific.

BTN.name: Bhutan
BTN.summary:
Bhutan is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally (Pride Bhutan, Rainbow Bhutan). The government engages with UNFPA's Free & Equal campaign at the level of the Royal Court of Justice and Cabinet. Trans women report violence and discrimination remain widespread (trans people 4x more likely to experience assault), and there is no legal gender recognition, but there is no criminalisation, no police targeting pattern, and a monarchy-led culture that discourages open aggression.

Tourism is tightly regulated (daily fee system), which incidentally provides visitors a structured, monitored environment.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021; LGBTIQ organisations can register (though the process is lengthy). No stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit SOGISC protections; legal gender recognition is unavailable in practice, though authorities previously allowed some changes.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service (Nov 2024): 'Trans women face hurdles in reporting violence' - trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report assaults, family pressure to 'accept it as fate', and laws that 'only cater to men and women'.

UNFPA Bhutan report 'Fostering Awareness: Advancing LGBT+ Rights & Inclusivity in Bhutan' (March 2025, 37pp): the 2024 Free & Equal campaign advanced LGBTIQ+ equality among policymakers, parliamentarians and institutions (Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General, Cabinet Secretariat), securing the first direct dialogue between the LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians in Bhutan's history.

Erasing 76 Crimes (June 2019): Bhutan's lower house voted nearly unanimously (43-1) to repeal the 'unnatural sex' provisions (Sections 213-214, punishable by 1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten: 'This is our first journey towards equality.'

Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2021): Bhutan's Penal Code Amendment Act came into force Feb 17, 2021 - after the upper house reinserted the provision, a joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex'; decriminalisation completed.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service feature: 'Black and White and the Colours of the Rainbow' - the emergence of Bhutan's LGBT community via the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page; profiles of administrators and Dechen, one of only two trans women living publicly (who fought to wear a kira to school at 16); notes self-stigma is significant but discrimination 'not very widespread'.

The Daily Beast (Oct 2015): 'Gay in Nirvana' - Bhutan's small LGBT population has experienced very little persecution or violence, but the concept of being gay or trans is 'pretty much unheard of'; no shared language for these identities; lesbianism under-recognised; Karma Dupchen created the first public LGBT outlet (LGBT Bhutan Facebook page) in 2013.

BTN.tangentialFactors: The 2021 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
BTN.localsOnly: No legal gender recognition — resident-facing; the 4x assault likelihood and violence/discrimination reports describe residents' experience.
BTN.comparisons: Pairwise: above Nepal (0.64 — Nepal has stronger jurisprudence but Bhutan lower reported violence) and below Romania (0.67).

LAO.name: Laos
LAO.summary: Laos is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, and Laos has a socially visible tradition of trans feminine people; but there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, no registered LGBT organisation (the one-party state restricts all civil society), and no documented recourse. Vientiane and Luang Prabang are accustomed to tourists; the risk is administrative (an opaque state) more than violent.

TLS.name: Timor-Leste
TLS.summary: Timor-Leste is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's equality provisions have been read inclusively, and Dili hosts an annual Pride march with government participation — remarkable for a young, Catholic-majority nation. There is no legal gender recognition and services are thin, but there is no documented pattern of police targeting or anti-trans violence, and the small community (CODIVA, Arco Iris) operates openly.
TLS.outOfScopeNotes: Service thinness and LGR absence are resident-facing.

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea
PNG.summary:
Papua New Guinea is High Risk for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years), and PNG has extreme levels of gender-based violence generally — among the world's highest documented rates. Port Moresby and Lae are dangerous cities for everyone; tribal-justice dynamics and police brutality affect marginalised people severely. There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and sorcery-accusation violence shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

For a visitor: the trans-specific risk is inseparable from the general security situation, which is among the worst in the Pacific.
PNG.outOfScopeNotes: General security conditions affect all travelers severely; criminalisation is the trans-relevant mechanism.

BWA.name: Botswana
BWA.summary:
Botswana is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — Africa's strongest judicial record after South Africa. The High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2019 (Letsweletse Motshidiemang v AG, upheld 2021); the Court of Appeal ordered the government to register LEGABIBO; and trans people have won document-change cases (ND v Attorney General, 2017). Draft 2024 constitutional changes even contemplate intersex rights. Implementation lags the rulings (SALC documents unsatisfactory compliance), social conservatism persists, and there is no general LGR statute — but the courts are a genuine protection, unique in the region.

For a visitor: decriminalised, functioning courts, moderate social hostility.

NAM.name: Namibia
NAM.summary:
Namibia is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Courts have delivered important rulings (the 2023 Digashu recognition of foreign same-sex marriages; earlier document-change wins for trans people), but same-sex conduct between men technically remains criminalised under the common law (the 2024 High Court declined to strike it, and parliament passed hostile marriage bills), and implementation of pro-LGBT rulings is documented as unsatisfactory (SALC). Windhoek has a small organised community (Equal Namibia); police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: enforcement of the old law is essentially nil, but the legal floor is hostile and the politics are deteriorating.
NAM.outOfScopeNotes: Common-law criminalisation is unenforced but real; implementation gaps are resident-facing.

MUS.name: Mauritius
MUS.summary:
Mauritius is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — the Indian Ocean's most liveable jurisdiction. The Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct; the Equal Opportunities Act covers discrimination; and in 2024 Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan competed as the first trans woman in Miss Universe Mauritius — a public milestone met with national discussion rather than violence. There is no legal gender recognition law (a barrier highlighted by AfricLaw), and social conservatism persists, but tourist infrastructure is extensive and accustomed to diverse visitors, and there is no documented police targeting pattern.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning courts, low street risk in tourist areas.
MUS.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and recognition gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): the Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct - advances for LGB people, less evident for trans/intersex people. No same-sex marriage; the Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against sexual-orientation discrimination; intersex children can be registered as 'undetermined' (2021 Civil Status Act) but nonconsensual procedures not banned; Pride since 2005 with counter-protests; some anti-LGBTIQ hate speech during 2024 elections.

AfricLaw (Aug 2024) by Lakshmi Kanhiya: Miss Universe Mauritius 2024 - the historic participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan as the first trans woman contestant marks a milestone; the article discusses the broader legal and social challenges for trans people in Mauritius (Civil Status Act 1981, Central Population Database, stigmatisation, lack of legal recognition).
US State Department 2016 Human Rights Report for Mauritius: official assessment - sodomy law (Section 250) rarely enforced; societal discrimination exists; no legal gender recognition.

Young Queer Alliance policy brief (July 2021): 'Administrative recognition of Trans People in Mauritius' - argues for legal gender recognition; notes the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders (2019) and calls on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law.

US Mission in Geneva (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - US diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the Human Rights Council, relevant to Mauritius's international human-rights environment.

MUS.tangentialFactors: The 2023 decriminalisation ruling removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
MUS.localsOnly: No LGR law — resident-facing gap highlighted by AfricLaw.
MUS.comparisons: Pairwise: below Seychelles-region comparators and level with Latvia (0.69)/Israel (0.69) — above Hungary (0.68).

SYC.name: Seychelles
SYC.summary: Seychelles is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016; the constitution guarantees equal protection; and the country is a small, tourism-dependent archipelago with extremely low violent crime and long exposure to international visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-specific infrastructure, but also no documented pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.
SYC.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence is resident-facing; evidence is thin given the tiny population.

LiquiSearch (Wikipedia-derived): LGBT rights in Seychelles - pre-repeal snapshot noting male 'carnal knowledge against the order of nature' was illegal while female same-sex acts were legal.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Sept 2024): 'Formerly an anti-gay haven, Seychelles becomes a protector of its LGBTQ citizens' - the new Penal Code (Amendment) Bill (18-8) increases sentences for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability; HDT: after South Africa, the second African country protecting against all forms of hate-based victimisation.

SEN.name: Senegal
SEN.summary:
Senegal is High Risk for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “unnatural acts” (up to 5 years, applied to both men and women), enforcement is active (periodic arrest waves), and anti-LGBT forces are pushing to raise sentences to 15 years. Mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented, and even public discussion is policed: two men were jailed in 2024 for “false news” after accusing the Prime Minister of tolerating homosexuality. There is no legal gender recognition and no visible community infrastructure — Dakar's scene is deeply underground.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest and mob violence.
SEN.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; mob violence is documented climate.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity (Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, up to 5 years' imprisonment). (Only the opening of the profile was retrievable at fetch time.)

Erasing 76 Crimes (July 2024): anti-LGBT forces in Senegal seek longer prison time - after PM Sonko alleged homosexuality is 'tolerated', MP Cheikh Abdou Bara Dolly Mbacké proposed a bill mirroring a failed 2022 initiative raising sentences to 10-15 years for 'offences of bisexuality [including homosexuality], transsexuality, necrophilia and zoophilia' plus fines up to 5 million CFA francs; abuses against LGBT+ people are commonplace.

BBC (June 2024): two men jailed in Senegal for 'spreading false news' after accusing PM Sonko of tolerating homosexuality - activist Bah Diakhate and Imam Ndao received three months and fines; Sonko had said homosexuality was 'not accepted, but tolerated' after a French politician expressed support for same-sex marriage at a Dakar student forum.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Senegal: documents preelectoral violence, torture, and 'violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons' among major human-rights problems.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Sept 2018): a wave of politically motivated anti-gay arrests as the 2019 election approached - two women and two men detained in Dakar for 'acts against the order of nature'; Arc en Ciel Senegal: 'The hunt for sexual minorities begins' as the government defends itself against 'pro-homosexual' accusations; Pan Africa ILGA called for accountability.
Metro (Nov 2023): a man's body was exhumed and set on fire in the street after locals found out he was gay - a case that shocked Senegal, where homosexuality is punishable with prison time.

SEN.tangentialFactors: “Unnatural acts” criminalised (up to 5 years, both sexes) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
SEN.comparisons: Pairwise: below Malaysia (0.28 — comparable criminalisation-plus-mob climate) and above Pakistan (0.26) and Côte d'Ivoire (0.34 — CIV decriminalised but has the 2024 hunt-down violence wave; SEN has statutory criminalisation but no equivalent mob-hunt wave; net SEN slightly worse).

CIV.name: Côte d'Ivoire
CIV.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is High Risk for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Long considered West Africa's tolerant outlier (same-sex conduct has never been criminalised), the country saw a wave of violence in late 2024: social-media influencers exhorted followers to “hunt” gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed (NYT, Oct 2024). There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection; police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in Abidjan.
CIV.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 violence wave targeted perceived gay men primarily but gender-nonconforming people are the most visible targets.

MLI.name: Mali
MLI.summary:
Mali is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.
MLI.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 penal code application to trans expression is via indecency provisions; drafting vagueness noted by HDT.

BFA.name: Burkina Faso
BFA.summary:
Burkina Faso is High Risk for trans visitors. In July 2024 the military junta approved a revised Personal and Family Code criminalising homosexuality — Burkina Faso had never previously outlawed it. The junta (Traoré) has clamped down on opposition and media, promised elections have not been held, and much of the country faces jihadist insurgency. Enforcement details of the new law remain unclear (HDT notes drafting uncertainty), but the direction and the absence of any institutional recourse are unambiguous.

For a visitor: new criminalisation under a junta, plus severe general security conditions.
BFA.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 family-code criminalisation is new; enforcement practice not yet documented.

sources.summary: BBC (July 2024): Burkina Faso's military junta approved legislation to ban homosexual acts - previously not outlawed though socially frowned upon. Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala announced the cabinet approval as part of a marriage-law overhaul that recognises only religious and customary marriages; the law still needed passage by the military-controlled parliament and junta leader Traoré's signature.

Africanews (July 2024): the junta approved revised marriage-family legislation criminalising homosexuality with 'severe penalties', as part of the same overhaul recognising only religious and customary marriages. (Article body largely behind page furniture at fetch time.)

MOZ.name: Mozambique
MOZ.summary:
Mozambique is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — one of Africa's better legal positions. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 Penal Code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register (Lambda Mozambique); and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. RWA.name: Rwanda
RWA.summary:
Rwanda is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations). There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and civil society operates within the regime's tight limits.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil.

AGO.name: Angola
AGO.summary: Angola is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.

COD.name: DR Congo
COD.summary:
DR Congo is High Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised — but the reality on the ground is severe insecurity: mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented, police extortion is routine, the east is an active conflict zone (M23), and LGBT organisations (Savie asbl in Bukavu) report systematic violations in their 2024 UPR submission. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure; Kinshasa's small scene is underground.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but outing risks mob violence with no effective state protection anywhere in the country.

ZWE.name: Zimbabwe
ZWE.summary:

The 2006 Criminal Law Act criminalises sodomy (up to 1 year — a lighter formal penalty than neighbours, though indecency provisions add exposure), and Amnesty's 2024 report documents shrinking civic space threatening LGBT organising (GALZ operates under pressure; its offices have been raided historically). For a visitor: statutory exposure exists but enforcement is sporadic; social hostility is the main risk.

Discrimination and violence are regular despite the moratorium.

SDN.name: Sudan
SDN.summary:
Sudan is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Article 152 of the Penal Code criminalises gender nonconformity directly; sodomy carries life imprisonment (capital/corporal punishment removed in 2020 reforms); and Cairo 52 documents state violence against LGBTQIA+ people including extrajudicial killings. Since April 2023 the country has been in a catastrophic civil war (SAF vs RSF) with documented mass atrocities — the conflict intensifies every risk and eliminates any recourse. There is no LGR and no community infrastructure.

For a visitor: statutory criminalisation of gender nonconformity plus one of the world's worst active conflicts.
SDN.outOfScopeNotes: War conditions affect all; Art 152 is trans-specific.

SSD.name: South Sudan
SSD.summary:
South Sudan is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The 2008 Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years), and Human Dignity Trust lists South Sudan as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. The country has barely emerged from civil war, state institutions are vestigial outside Juba, communal violence is endemic, and there is no documented LGBT community infrastructure whatsoever — no organisation can operate openly. No trans-specific case is documented because documentation itself is nearly impossible.

For a visitor: statutory risk plus a near-total absence of protective institutions.
SSD.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation absence reflects state incapacity; gender-expression criminalisation is statutory.

SOM.name: Somalia
SOM.summary:
Somalia is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — one of the world's most dangerous countries for any LGBT person. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 3 years), but the operative reality is worse: Al-Shabaab controls significant territory and applies its interpretation of sharia, under which homosexuality and gender transgression are capital offences — executions are documented. Even in government areas, mob violence and clan-justice dynamics make any gender nonconformity lethal-risk. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, and no recourse of any kind.

For a visitor: there is no safe way to be visibly trans anywhere in Somalia.
SOM.outOfScopeNotes: Fragmented authority means enforcement varies; Al-Shabaab areas apply capital punishment.

ERI.name: Eritrea
ERI.summary: Eritrea is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Article 310(1) of the 2015 Penal Code criminalises “homosexual conduct” (up to 7 years), there are no anti-discrimination protections of any kind, and Eritrea is among the world's most closed states — indefinite national service, mass arbitrary detention, no independent media, no civil society, and no way to document conditions. Eritrea has rejected every SOGI recommendation at every UPR cycle. Nothing is known about trans people in Eritrea because nothing can be known — the absence of data reflects total informational control.
ERI.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation absence reflects totalitarian informational control.

WSM.name: Samoa
WSM.summary:
Samoa is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — anchored by one of the world's most institutionalized third-gender traditions. Fa'afafine (and fa'atama) are culturally embedded: recognized as heirs to customary land and eligible for matai (chiefly) titles within fa'a Sāmoa, organized nationally through the Samoa Fa'afafine Association (a formal UN UPR stakeholder since 1987), and visible through a famous pageant culture. Samoa repealed its colonial-era “female impersonation” crime in 2013, so no law touches gender expression itself.

The remaining negatives are modest for a visitor: no anti-discrimination law and no legal gender recognition (both resident-facing); documented discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against fa'afafine (APTN peer-led study — primarily resident/domestic contexts); isolated police-harassment reports (2 respondents, no convictions); and village fono councils that enforce conservative dress and behaviour norms. The unenforced sodomy statute is a situational risk for a fraction of visitors, not a trans-universal one.
WSM.outOfScopeNotes: Fa’afafine cultural embedding is informal protection; criminalisation unenforced.

TON.name: Tonga
TON.summary: Tonga is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. The Criminal Offences Act criminalises sodomy (10 years, plus corporal punishment on paper — unenforced in recent years) and also criminalises males “impersonating a female” while soliciting — a direct trans-expression statute on the books. Against that: Tonga has a visible leiti (trans-feminine) community with the famous Miss Galaxy pageant (documented by the Washington Post in 2024), family and church networks that are devout but not systematically violent, and no documented recent prosecutions.
TON.outOfScopeNotes: The male-impersonation statute is on the books but unenforced.

BEN.name: Benin

sources.summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (April 2024): interview with Luc Agblakou, founder of the Hirondelles Club in Benin, which since 2013 has supported LGBT+ people with housing - founded after a father murdered his gay son. Nearly 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed through its 20-place temporary accommodation centre; the organisation now has branches in Togo, Burkina Faso and Niger. Article notes anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations are not criminalised in Benin, but there is no SOGISC discrimination protection, no legal gender recognition, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. LGBTIQ people face stigma from the public and police, which cracked down on a 'network of homosexuals' in 2022. The 2021 Benin Human Rights Commission report flagged physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention, torture and degrading treatment against LGBTQI+ people; LBQ women rarely report violence to police.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Benin: official assessment including the section on acts of violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity - same-sex conduct not criminalised but no protections; documents societal stigma and police treatment.

MRT.name: Mauritania
MRT.summary: Mauritania is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — one of the world's most dangerous legal environments. There is no LGR, no healthcare, no community, and sharia courts operate alongside the civil system.

MDV.name: Maldives
MDV.summary:
Maldives is High Risk for trans visitors — a sharp resort/local split. Under the Penal Code and sharia framework, same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 8 years, with 100 lashes available), and gender-nonconforming Maldivians face prosecution and social erasure; activists operate from exile (a 2024 HRC shadow report documents ICCPR violations). BUT: the tourist resort islands operate as a legally distinct world — no LGBT tourist is documented as prosecuted on a resort; the risk concentrates in Malé and local islands.

A resort-only visit is lower-risk than the score suggests; any local-island contact raises it.
MDV.outOfScopeNotes: Resort islands are de-facto insulated; the score reflects the national legal framework and local-island exposure.

PRK.name: North Korea
PRK.summary: North Korea is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is not named in the Criminal Code — but Article 193 prohibits “decadent culture,” and broad provisions on obscene activities give authorities unlimited discretion; reported incidents of criminalisation and even execution for homosexuality exist. The concept of gender identity simply does not exist in public life (BBC Korea: sexual minorities are “denied as a concept”). Tourists are under constant escort and surveillance; any nonconforming presentation or discovered digital material risks detention in the world's most totalitarian system.

ESH.summary:

GMB.name: Gambia
GMB.summary: Gambia is High Risk for trans visitors. There is no LGR and no visible community.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Gambia has criminalised same-sex conduct since the colonial era; the 2014 amendment introduced 'aggravated homosexuality' (life imprisonment) under Jammeh, who threatened to 'decapitate' gay people. A new criminal code (March 2025) removes 'aggravated homosexuality' but sets a minimum of five years for 'unnatural offences' (defined as 'any homosexual act') and three years for 'gross indecency', with no maximum - so any same-sex act could in theory draw life. The Barrow government has not typically enforced.
